## Media Planning and Buying 
The firm will lead the development, implementation, and ongoing optimization of an evidence-based media program designed to advance the City’s tourism objectives and ensure intentional, responsible stewardship of public funds. This work includes recommendations on priority audiences, geographic markets, seasonal timing, channel mix, campaign phasing, and budget allocation, based on available research, destination conditions, travel-planning windows, audience receptivity, media costs, visitor value, and expected incremental benefit.
Recommendations should consider not only the potential volume of visitation but also visitor value, potential length of stay, repeat visitation, and opportunities to distribute visitor spending across Palm Desert’s tourism-related sectors. The firm will negotiate, place, traffic, monitor, reconcile, and report on media; use performance information to test strategic hypotheses; and proactively move funds away from underperforming tactics when stronger opportunities are identified.
The City will approve the overall media strategy, geographic markets, major channels, campaign creative, and budget. The firm may make routine tactical optimizations within approved guardrails, but prior City approval is required for material changes, including shifting expenditures between geographic markets, abandoning an approved channel or platform, or changing approved creative or messaging. Material changes will be documented through a brief written summary, which may be handled by email.
The firm shall maintain a City-approved media plan or media authorization identifying planned expenditures by market, channel, platform, campaign, and applicable period. Media shall not be placed in excess of authorized amounts. The firm shall provide periodic expenditure reports comparing authorized, committed, invoiced, and remaining working-media funds and shall complete year-end or campaign-end reconciliation of all media expenditures.
Media-planning and management services will be included within the annual services not-to-exceed amount, while the City’s working-media budget will be treated as a separate pass-through expense billed at actual net cost. No markup, commission, rebate, incentive, credit, or other compensation derived from media placement will be permitted. The firm will maintain transparent records sufficient for the City to verify placements, costs, performance, optimization decisions, and reconciliation of public funds.

## Public Relations and Earned Media 
The firm will provide destination public-relations and earned-media capability and will recommend the role that these services should play within the City’s overall tourism-marketing program and annual services budget. Depending on the approved annual work plan, this work may include identifying newsworthy destination stories and opportunities; developing media strategies, pitches, press materials, and supporting content; cultivating relationships with relevant travel, lifestyle, regional, and trade media; responding to qualified media inquiries; coordinating interviews, itineraries, familiarization opportunities, and destination information; and integrating earned-media activity with paid media, creative, social media, tourism email communications, major events, and partner activity.
The City has not established a minimum annual allocation or fixed level of public-relations activity. Proposers should recommend whether the program should be ongoing, seasonal, project-based, or opportunity-driven and explain the expected value, limitations, and opportunity costs of that recommendation. Annual priorities, activity levels, deliverables, and allocations may vary through the annual work plan.
The firm will promptly refer to City staff any matter involving City policy, official statements, sensitive issues, political matters, legal concerns, public safety, crisis communications, or material reputational risk. The firm shall not issue statements, respond on the City’s behalf, or provide crisis-communications or governmental public-information services unless expressly directed and separately authorized by the City. Such matters will remain under City direction and approval.
This category is intended to support proactive destination storytelling and earned-media visibility and does not transfer the City’s governmental public-information or crisis-communications responsibilities to the firm.

## Research, Measurement, and Analytics 
The firm will lead the research and measurement strategy needed to inform tourism-marketing decisions, evaluate performance, and improve the City’s use of public funds. This work includes identifying appropriate research and data needs; using available audience, market, media, social, email, website, destination, and economic information to develop and test strategic hypotheses; establishing practical performance measures and reporting frameworks; interpreting results; and recommending changes to strategy, creative, media, content, and annual priorities.
The firm will coordinate measurement across paid media, social media, tourism email communications, website activity, and other approved initiatives, with particular attention to the City’s priority conversion proxies, including email signups, qualified outbound clicks to partner and event websites, and engaged trip-planning behavior. The firm will also recommend a practical Google Analytics 4 (GA4) event and measurement framework, while the City’s webmaster or other technical resource will remain responsible for technical implementation.
Measurement should connect marketing performance, where reasonably possible, to broader destination and economic indicators such as lodging demand, occupancy, room rates, visitor spending, and Transient Occupancy Tax trends. The firm should establish meaningful performance measures, assess return on marketing investment where reliable data and attribution methods permit, identify appropriate proxy or modeled measures where direct attribution is not feasible, and use findings to continuously improve investment decisions.
Primary consumer, audience, market, or brand-health research may be conducted selectively rather than annually, as established in the annual work plan. When brand-health research is undertaken, the firm should preserve key benchmark questions over time while allowing additional questions aligned with current strategic needs. The City will retain ownership and administrative control of research purchased with City funds, analytics accounts, advertising accounts where feasible, pixels, tags, data, dashboards, and related institutional records.
This category is intended to produce useful decision-making insights rather than reporting volume for its own sake, and it does not require the firm to guarantee direct attribution of visitation, bookings, or economic impact where the City does not control the transaction.

The firm shall incorporate accessibility into the development of materials within its control, including, as applicable, accessible document formatting, readable typography, sufficient color contrast, alternative text, captions, transcripts, and other accessibility features appropriate to the communication format. The firm shall coordinate with City staff regarding accessibility requirements for materials requiring City review, publication, or technical implementation.

Examples may include major destination events, special promotional initiatives, one-time research or creative projects, supplemental media programs, or other tourism-marketing opportunities requiring services within one or more of the scope categories identified in this RFP.
Special Projects and Emerging Opportunities are outside of the annual $335,000 firm-services not-to-exceed amount identified in this RFP and would be considered Extra Work.
Subject to available funding, applicable City authorization requirements, and the terms of the resulting Agreement, the City may request that the selected firm develop a separate proposed scope, schedule, and budget for such work. No Special Project or Emerging Opportunity shall proceed without prior written City authorization, and any additional compensation shall be separately approved in accordance with the Aggrement and applicable City requirements. 
The City reserves the right to procure services separately when it determines that a project falls outside the competitively procured scope, requires materially different expertise, is subject to separate funding or procurement requirements, or would otherwise be more appropriately procured independently.

## Minimum Program Deliverables
At a minimum, the firm will provide the following deliverables, subject to refinement through the approved annual work plan:
An annual tourism-marketing strategy, work plan, budget allocation, implementation schedule, and measurement framework;
Campaign, creative, media, content, public-relations, and research recommendations sufficient to implement the approved annual program;
Appropriate plans, calendars, briefs, schedules, budgets, and approval materials for work undertaken under each applicable Scope of Services category;
Routine budget, project-status, media-performance, channel-performance, and program-level reporting;
Timely reconciliation and supporting documentation for media and other approved pass-through expenditures;
An annual performance assessment identifying key findings, strategic implications, and recommendations regarding what the City should continue, change, test, or discontinue; and
Organized delivery and transfer of City-owned creative files, research, data, account information, reporting records, and other work products.
Routine reporting shall generally include monthly budget and project-status reporting; periodic campaign and channel-performance reporting appropriate to the activity being measured; and at least an annual program-level performance assessment and an annual marketing strategies session with the City Council. The City and firm may consolidate reporting where doing so improves usefulness and avoids duplicative reporting.
The firm shall maintain City work products, files, credentials, records, and account information in an organized manner throughout the engagement so that City staff can reasonably access and transition such materials without dependence upon individual firm personnel.
The annual work plan will establish the specific deliverables, quantities, timing, service levels, and budget allocations for each contract year. Deliverable volumes may vary based on approved strategy, available funding, performance evidence, campaign needs, and City priorities.

## Proposal Planning Context
For purposes of proposal planning, Proposers should assume that the City’s tourism-marketing program will include year-round destination marketing with seasonal variation in activity; paid media activity in multiple geographic markets, including major California metropolitan areas and at least one significant out-of-state market; development and ongoing application of a destination campaign platform across paid media, social media, email, and other tourism-marketing channels; periodic photography and video production; and ongoing management of the Discover Palm Desert social media program. Use meaningful public, stakeholder, agency, and interdepartmental engagement and show how input influenced the plan.
Equity Considerations
Identify disproportionate safety burdens and incorporate equity into analysis, engagement, prioritization, and evaluation of recommended projects and strategies.
Policy and Process Changes
Assess City policies, standards, workflows, practices, and decision-making processes and identify changes that will better prioritize transportation safety.
Strategy and Project Selections
Identify and prioritize a comprehensive set of infrastructure, behavioral, operational, policy, programmatic, and other Safe System strategies and projects, with transparent criteria and implementation timeframes.
Progress and Transparency
Establish measures, data practices, responsibilities, and an accessible annual reporting approach for tracking progress after adoption.
 
Beyond minimum SS4A compliance, the City is especially interested in a consultant approach that:
Moves the Safe System Approach from a planning concept into everyday City decision-making, including responding to traffic safety concerns and collisions, capital planning, project development, design, operations, maintenance, funding, development review, and other relevant workflows.
Combines reactive crash analysis with proactive, systemic risk analysis and clearly explains where and why severe crashes are most likely to occur.
Produces an implementation-ready list of priority projects, programs, policies, and strategies, with an appropriate level of concept development to position high-priority improvements for future funding and delivery. Consultants should recommend the level and quantity of concept development that will provide the greatest value within the available budget.
Identifies policy or process changes that can begin during the planning effort, rather than deferring all implementation until after plan adoption.
Creates tools and workflows that City staff can maintain and use after the consultant contract ends.

## Task 2 – Neighborhood Traffic Management Program Evaluation and Update
The City's Neighborhood Traffic Management Program has been in place for nearly 20 years and has historically served as the mechanism for neighborhood traffic calming requests and installation of treatments such as speed humps. The City seeks a substantive evaluation and update of the program.
The consultant should recommend a modernized program that, at a minimum, considers:
The current state of practice in neighborhood traffic calming and speed management.
The effectiveness, equity, transparency, and administrative efficiency of the City's existing request, evaluation, prioritization, engagement, and implementation processes.
A more systematic and proactive approach to identifying and addressing neighborhood safety needs.
Evaluation of a selection of previously installed traffic calming projects to inform an updated toolbox
An updated toolbox that includes permanent treatments, quick-build or low-cost approaches, and appropriate implementation pathways.
How neighborhood traffic calming should relate to the City's broader Safe System strategy, High Injury Network, active transportation goals, Safe Routes to School, and Complete Streets guidance.
A practical implementation and funding approach that can be administered by City staff over time.

## Task 3 – Traffic Safety Data Demonstration
The City has grant funding for a demonstration activity involving traffic safety data software. The City does not have a predetermined software product or solution in mind. The demonstration should begin by defining the problem and the information gap, not by selecting a product and then creating a use case for it.
Demonstration Framework
Define the need  ->  Define the capability  ->  Identify potential solutions  ->  Test and evaluate  ->  Institutionalize what works
 
The consultant should use this workstream as a structured but flexible sandbox for testing how better data, software, analytical tools, or related technology can improve City safety decisions. The selected approach should:
Identify gaps, delays, limitations, or inefficiencies in the City's current safety data and decision-making processes.
Translate those gaps into clearly defined functional needs or capabilities before screening solutions.
Research and recommend commercially available or otherwise SS4A-eligible solutions that fit the approved grant scope.
Design and support a finite demonstration with clear evaluation measures and data collection.
Evaluate usefulness, limitations, cost, staff burden, scalability, and decision-making value.
Recommend how successful tools, data, or information should be incorporated into ongoing City workflows, staffing, budgeting, and future safety analysis.
Feed lessons from the demonstration back into the TSAP and future project/strategy selection.

## Engagement, Communication, and Collaboration
Engagement will happen throughout the previously listed tasks. Based on the Consultants vision, the project team will develop an efficient engagement structure that satisfies SS4A requirements, reflects Rancho Cordova's community, reaches relevant agencies and stakeholders, and produces information that improves the plan and/or creates community support.
The Consultant should identify where engagement can be coordinated with the Complete Streets Implementation Guide and where separate conversations are warranted. The City anticipates opportunities for shared technical advisory meetings, stakeholder discussions, internal staff workshops, and public engagement, but does not assume that all activities must be combined.
Public-facing products should be clear, accessible, concise, and visually compelling. The City values strong data visualization, maps, graphics, and storytelling that make technical safety information understandable to nontechnical audiences.

## Expected Deliverables
The City expects the following major deliverables. Consultants may propose additional or alternative deliverables or a different packaging of technical work if it better supports the proposed process. The City does not require a separate memorandum for every work element.
Project work plan, schedule, budget, quality-control approach, and coordination framework with the Complete Streets Implementation Guide.
High Injury Network and supporting safety analysis, including documented methodology, GIS data, and other source files necessary for future City updates.
Draft and Final Traffic Safety Action Plan satisfying the applicable FY24 SS4A Action Plan components, including a priority project list, an implementation and prioritization framework, and an ongoing progress/transparency approach.
Updated Neighborhood Traffic Management Program materials, including the program framework, process, prioritization approach, engagement approach, and traffic management toolbox necessary for implementation.
Demonstration plan, evaluation results, and recommendations for how successful data/software capabilities should be incorporated into future City processes.
Engagement and collaboration record documenting who was engaged, what was learned, and how input influenced key decisions.
Presentation materials for key decision points, City leadership, and City Council, as appropriate.
All final editable/native files, data, GIS layers, graphics, and source materials necessary for the City to maintain and use the work after contract completion.

- Team and Relevant Experience: 25
- Integration with the Complete Streets Implementation Guide & Collaborative Approach: 25
- Work Plan, Schedule & Project Management: 15

## Scope of Work
Task 1:  Existing Conditions & Document Review
Data Needs and Standards Inventory:
Building on datasets and analyses from the Rancho Cordova Active Transportation Plan (ATP) to be completed in early 2026, the project team will identify and compile data from the City of Rancho Cordova, SACOG, Caltrans District 3, Sacramento Regional Transit, and Sacramento County. Key datasets will include collisions, speeds, right-of-way mapping, roadway classifications, traffic volumes, transit facilities, pedestrian and bicycle networks, ADA compliance, and demographic indicators such as CalEnviroScreen 4.0 and the Healthy Places Index. Data standards will be established to ensure consistency across GIS layers.
An inventory of design standards will compile relevant documents that influence the design of the public right-of-way, including City Street Design Standards, County Street Standards, City Code, General Plan Circulation Element Policies, regional Stomrwater Quality Design Manual, SacRT transit standards, Metro Fire design standards, and others.
State of the Practice and Document Review:
The team will review the City’s General Plan, Climate Action Plan, Active Transportation Plan, Local Road Safety Plan, and development standards, along with SACOG and Caltrans guidance. The audit will identify opportunities to align City policies with Caltrans Complete Streets Policy (DP-37) and CAPTI.
Additionally, the project team will review about ten local jurisdictions complete streets guides to extract lessons learned and best practices by peer cities who are leading the way in implementing complete streets effectively.
Goals and Objectives:
Based on the data and policy review, the project team will define goals and objectives focused on safety, accessibility, and sustainability while addressing multimodal and equity gaps citywide.
Documentation of Existing Conditions:
Field verification will document current conditions, safety issues, and barriers to multimodal travel. Photographs, GPS data, and notes will be compiled in a GIS database to illustrate infrastructure gaps and priority areas. 
Task Deliverables
Existing Conditions Report summarizing findings from data analysis, fieldwork, and policy review.
Inventory of Existing Transportation Facilities including pedestrian, bicycle, transit, and roadway infrastructure
Peer City review of best practices plus goals and objectives of the Guide
 
Task 2:  Community & Stakeholders Engagement
This task will ensure meaningful participation from community members, local organizations, and agency partners throughout the development of the Rancho Cordova Complete Streets Implementation Guide, consistent with CalSTA’s 
Climate Action Plan for Transportation Infrastructure (CAPTI)
 Strategy 3, “Elevate Community Voices.” Due to the technical nature of street design standards, the project team will have to develop creative ways to extract feedback from the general public that will be translated into more technical deliverables.
Engagement Plan:
The project team will prepare an Engagement Plan outlining strategies and a schedule to reach residents across all neighborhoods, especially underserved communities. The Engagement will blend different voices, forums, and approaches in order to receive the needed input (defined further in the following paragraphs). Many of the specific touch points will be detailed as the project progresses, allowing for adaptability. Nevertheless, at a minimum the project will host three Project Working Group Meetings, four Stakeholder Interviews, and five pop-up events, walking/biking tours, or workshops. Three of the five community-focused events will be in our under-resourced communities. Walking/biking tours historically have worked well in under-resourced communities. We’ll leverage connections with the community Food Hub, faith-based groups, and parent organizations at the schools to expand our reach.
Project Working Group Meetings:
The City will convene a Project Working Group (PWG) with a cross section of City staff and agency partner staff such as Caltrans District 3, SACOG, Sacramento Regional Transit, Cordova Recreation and Park District, and Metro Fire to guide the development of the Guide. The PWG will review the technical nature of the design development.  
Stakeholder Interviews and Coordination:
Focused interviews and coordination meetings will be held with and in collaboration with Cordova Recreation and Park District, 50 Corridor TMA, and community organizations like Civic Thread, schools, parent groups, and advocacy partners to identify local priorities and challenges.
Community Engagement Events and Meetings:
Engagement events, including pop-ups, workshops, and walking and bicycling tours, will be held citywide throughout the development of the Guide. Surveys and interactive online tools will allow residents to share feedback during three key project milestones: existing conditions, draft framework, and public draft review.
City Leadership and Council Updates:
City staff will provide regular updates to City leadership and the City Council to maintain transparency and alignment with community goals.
A project website will share updates and project development milestones. This inclusive approach will ensure that community perspectives directly shape the Guide’s priorities, design guidelines, and implementation strategies.
Task Deliverables
Community Engagement Plan 
Project Working Group roster and meeting notes 
Project Website
Minimum: 3 Project Working Group meetings, 4 stakeholder interviews, and 5 community events (3 in under-resourced communities)
Community Meeting Materials, Surveys, and an engagement plan report documenting and summarizing activities, interview summaries, key findings, and how input informed the Guide.
 
Task 3:  Guidelines Development
This task will synthesize findings from Tasks 1 and 2 to develop a design and policy framework that standardizes Complete Streets practices across the City of Rancho Cordova. The framework will reflect community priorities, technical expertise, and guidance from State and regional partners.
Identify Needs Based on Community and Stakeholder Feedback:
The project team will integrate public input and feedback from the Technical Advisory Committee to identify key design and policy needs. Community priorities related to safety, comfort, and accessibility will guide the structure of the Complete Streets Implementation Guide. This step will ensure that recommendations respond to the conditions and opportunities identified through the Existing Conditions and Engagement tasks.
Create Guide Outline and Illustration Needs:
The team will prepare an outline of the Guide and identify the illustrations, maps, and graphics needed to convey context-sensitive design principles clearly. This will result in a set of context-sensitive street typologies that represent local, collector, and arterial streets across different environments. Each typology will include conceptual cross sections, design treatments, and key elements such as sidewalks, bikeways, transit lanes, medians, landscaping, and stormwater features.
Implementation Processes, Policy Recommendations, and Trade-offs:
The project team will develop implementation strategies and process recommendations that integrate Complete Streets principles into the City’s Capital Improvement Program, development review procedures, and engineering standards. The analysis will establish how to navigate trade-offs by using metrics to evaluate safety, equity, and sustainability outcomes, using indicators such as crash reduction potential, accessibility improvements, VMT reduction, and user comfort. Draft design concepts and policies will be reviewed with community partners and the PWG to test feasibility and refine guidance. Equity will remain central throughout this task, with specific design and investment strategies aimed at improving access and safety in under-resourced neighborhoods.
All recommendations will align with Caltrans Complete Streets Policy (DP-37), Caltrans DIB 94, the Climate Action Plan for Transportation Infrastructure (CAPTI), SACOG’s MTP/SCS 2050, and the City’s forthcoming Active Transportation Plan and General Plan Update to ensure consistency across local and regional systems.
 
Task Deliverables
Memo of the Needs Assessment and Guide Outline based on staff, agency partner, community, and stakeholder feedback
Draft trade-off or reconciliation process
 
Task 4:  Draft and Final Guidelines
Develop Guidelines and Referenced Standards:
Building on previous tasks, the project team will compile results from the existing conditions analysis, engagement outcomes, design outline into a comprehensive Complete Streets Implementation Guide. The Guide will include citywide street typologies, cross-sections, design details, procedure recommendations, and a post-project evaluation model for safety, equity, and climate goals. It will also include a selection of prioritized corridors that stand in most need of Complete Streets enhancements with high-level concept designs. Revisions and updates to other City documents and procedures such as dedication requirements may also be included.
Administrative Draft of Guidelines:
An Administrative Draft will be prepared for review by City staff and the PWG. The draft will feature maps, illustrations, and design examples. Feedback will be collected and used to prepare the Public Draft.
Public Draft of Guidelines:
The Public Draft will be released for community and stakeholder review through public meetings and an online comment period. Input from residents, partner agencies, and advocacy groups will be summarized and incorporated into the Final Guide.
Final Complete Streets Guidelines:
The final Guide will integrate all feedback and present the Rancho Cordova Complete Streets Implementation Guide. It will be an online resource that provides design guidance and points to existing standards, and processes on how to design, build, and manage within the right-of-way. It will include a funding strategy connecting projects and maintenance to grant funding programs such as ATP, HSIP, and SS4A and local revenue streams. 
Task Deliverables
Administrative Draft of the Complete Streets Guide for internal review by City staff and PWG
Public Draft of the Complete Streets Guide for community and stakeholder review
Final Rancho Cordova Complete Streets Implementation Guide

## Traffic Control 
Provisions for public convenience, public safety, traffic control, and hours of work shall conform to Sections 7-8 and 12 of the Sacramento County Standard Construction Specifications, Section 12, “Temporary Traffic Control,” of the State Standard Specifications, the CA/MUTCD, these Special Provisions, the Project Plans, and as directed by the City Engineer.
 
The Contractor shall be responsible for public safety and for maintaining traffic within the Project limits and on approaches to the Project throughout construction. 
 
Prior to performing work requiring a modification of existing traffic patterns, including lane closures, the Contractor shall prepare and submit a Traffic Control Plan for review and approval by the City Engineer. No work requiring a lane closure or modification of existing traffic patterns shall begin until the applicable Traffic Control Plan has been approved.
 
No full roadway closure will be permitted. When a single lane is closed and traffic is maintained through a reversible lane, the Contractor shall provide a minimum of two flaggers.
 
Lane Closures shall be within the following hours without exemptions: 
8:30AM to 3:30PM 
 
Failure to fully reopen all lanes to traffic by the hours mentioned above, as determined by the Engineer, shall result in liquidated damages of 
SEVENTY FIVE DOLLARS
 (
$75.00) per minute
.
 
All work requiring a lane closure, including polyester concrete placement and curing, installation of temporary pavement markers (TRPMs), removal of traffic control devices, and restoration of the roadway for public traffic, shall be completed within the permitted lane closure hours. 
 
The local Fire Department, Sheriff/Police Department, California Highway Patrol, and Regional Transit (if applicable) shall be notified 24 hours in advance of construction work. Construction area signs shall conform to the requirements of Section 12-3.07 “Construction Signs” of the Standard Construction Specifications. 
 
The Traffic Control Plan shall provide for vehicular, pedestrian, and bicycle access around or through the work area. Where work is performed within 200 feet of a signalized intersection, the Traffic Control Plan shall address maintenance and operation of the traffic signal.
 
Construction shall be suspended and no activities that interfere with public traffic shall be conducted on Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Veterans Day, during the four-day Thanksgiving weekend, or from December 21 through January 1, unless otherwise approved in writing by the City Engineer.
 
Construction shall not be permitted on weekends or holidays unless otherwise approved in writing by the City Engineer.
 
Minor deviations from the traffic control requirements, except the 3:30 pm lane reopening requirement, may be permitted upon written request by the Contractor and written approval by the City Engineer. The Contractor shall not implement any deviation prior to receiving written approval.
 
Pedestrian and Bicycle Access
The Contractor shall maintain pedestrian and bicycle access through or around the construction area in accordance with the approved Traffic Control Plan and applicable accessibility requirements.
 
Temporary pedestrian access routes shall be maintained in a safe and accessible condition and shall be kept clear of construction materials, equipment, debris, and other obstructions. Temporary surfaces shall be firm, stable, slip resistant, and free of abrupt vertical changes or other tripping hazards.
 
Where construction creates temporary drop-offs or other hazards adjacent to pedestrian, bicycle, or vehicular travel ways, the Contractor shall provide appropriate temporary traffic control devices, barriers, signs, and delineation in accordance with Section 12, “Temporary Traffic Control,” of the State Standard Specifications.
 
Any closure or detour of an existing pedestrian or bicycle route shall require prior written approval from the City Engineer. Requests shall be submitted in writing and shall identify the proposed duration, limits of closure, detour route, signing, temporary facilities, and safety measures.
 
Full compensation for maintaining pedestrian and bicycle access, including temporary facilities, signing, delineation, and approved detours, shall be considered as included in the contract Lump Sum price paid for Traffic Control Plan, and no additional compensation will be made therefor.
 
Portable Changeable Message Signs
The Contractor shall furnish, place, operate, maintain, relocate, and remove portable changeable message signs as required for lane closures or road closures and as directed by the City Engineer. Portable changeable message signs shall conform to Section 12, “Temporary Traffic Control,” of the State Standard Specifications.
 
The Contractor shall provide and maintain a minimum of two (2) portable changeable message signs for the duration of construction. Locations and messages shall be approved by the City Engineer prior to use.
 
Portable changeable message signs shall be fully operational prior to beginning work and during the duration of work.

LUMP SUM

## Description of Work
The work to be performed under this contract consists of furnishing all labor, materials, and equipment for the replacement of the asphalt concrete deck with a polyester concrete overlay at Horn Road Bridge overcrossing the Boyd Station Drainage Channel, conforming the approaches to the bridge to the polyester concrete overlay and restriping within the project limits. 
The Contractor shall coordinate with the City Engineer throughout the Project to accommodate any adjustments, as deemed necessary by the City Engineer.
 
Such other items or details not mentioned above or in the bid quantities that are required by the Plans and/or these General Provisions, shall be performed, placed, constructed, or installed in accordance with the Standard Construction Specifications or these General Provisions.

## Water Pollution Control Plan 
Water pollution control shall conform to Section 10-4, “Erosion Sediment and Water Pollution Control,” of the Standard Construction Specifications, Sacramento County’s “Erosion and Sediment Control Guidelines,” these Special Provisions, the Project Plans, applicable permits, and as directed by the City Engineer.
 
The Contractor shall prevent erosion and the discharge or transport of sediment, construction debris, asphalt materials, concrete materials, wash water, petroleum products, and other pollutants resulting from construction activities into storm drain facilities, drainage facilities, Boyd Station Drainage Channel, or other receiving waters.
 
The Contractor shall prepare a Water Pollution Control Plan identifying the Best Management Practices (BMPs) necessary to control erosion, sediment, and construction-related pollutants throughout the duration of the Project. The Water Pollution Control Plan shall conform to the applicable requirements of Sacramento County’s “Erosion and Sediment Control Guidelines.”
 
The Contractor shall submit the Water Pollution Control Plan to the City Engineer for review at least five (5) working days prior to the start of construction. The Contractor shall revise the Water Pollution Control Plan as directed by the City Engineer. Construction activities that have the potential to discharge sediment or other pollutants shall not begin until the applicable BMPs have been installed and are functioning as intended.
 
The Contractor shall furnish, install, inspect, maintain, repair, replace, and remove BMPs as necessary throughout construction. If the BMPs implemented by the Contractor fail to provide effective erosion, sediment, or water pollution control, the Contractor shall immediately implement additional or modified measures as necessary and as directed by the City Engineer. The Contractor shall be responsible for cleanup and corrective measures resulting from erosion, sedimentation, spills, or other pollutant discharges caused by the Contractor’s operations.
 
Fees and security deposits required by Sacramento County’s “Erosion and Sediment Control Guidelines,” if applicable, shall be the responsibility of the Contractor.
 
The City will obtain project-specific stormwater permits required to be obtained by the project owner, if applicable. The Contractor shall comply with all permit requirements applicable to the Contractor’s operations and shall provide all records, inspections, reports, and other documentation required from the Contractor for permit compliance.
 
Measurement and Payment
Water Pollution Control Plan shall be included in the 
LUMP SUM
 price and shall include full compensation for furnishing all labor, materials, tools, equipment, and incidentals necessary to prepare and revise the Water Pollution Control Plan; furnish, install, inspect, maintain, repair, replace, and remove BMPs; perform required cleanup and corrective measures; comply with applicable permit requirements; and perform all other work necessary for water pollution control as specified in the Standard Construction Specifications, these Special Provisions, the Project Plans, and as directed by the City Engineer, and no additional compensation will be allowed therefor.

## Bridge Deck Preparation 
Bridge deck preparation shall conform to Section 60-3.02, “Bridge Deck Preparation,” of the 2025 Caltrans Standard Specifications, these Special Provisions, the Project Plans, and as directed by the City Engineer.
 
The Contractor shall remove the existing asphalt concrete overlay from the bridge deck and prepare the existing concrete deck for placement of the polyester concrete overlay in accordance with Section 60-3.02 of the State Standard Specifications. Bridge deck preparation shall include removal of the existing asphalt concrete overlay, cleaning, abrasive blasting, removal of contaminants, and all other work necessary to provide a clean, sound, and properly prepared surface.
 
The Contractor is advised to review 
Attachment (B) HBP Geotechnical Report
 included in the Contract Documents for information regarding the existing asphalt concrete overlay thickness on the bridge deck.
 
Following removal of the existing asphalt concrete overlay, the bridge deck shall be evaluated for unsound concrete in accordance with Section 60-3.02C(5), “Remove Unsound Concrete,” of the State Standard Specifications. The City Engineer will determine the limits of unsound concrete requiring removal. Removal and repair of unsound concrete will be paid for under Remove and Replace Unsound Concrete (Contingency).
 
The Contractor shall protect the prepared bridge deck from contamination, precipitation, and construction traffic until placement of the polyester concrete overlay.
 
Measurement and Payment
No separate payment will be made for Bridge Deck Preparation. Full compensation for removal and disposal of the existing asphalt concrete overlay from the bridge deck, cleaning, abrasive blasting, surface preparation, protection of the prepared deck, and all labor, materials, tools, equipment, and incidentals necessary to complete Bridge Deck Preparation shall be considered included in the 
LUMP SUM
 price paid for Polyester Concrete Overlay, and no additional compensation will be made therefor.

## Polyester Concrete Overlay 
Polyester Concrete Overlay shall conform to Section 60-3.02, “Bridge Deck Preparation,” and Section 60-3.04B, “Polyester Concrete Overlays,” of the 2025 Caltrans Standard Specifications, these Special Provisions, the Project Plans, and as directed by the City Engineer. Polyester concrete shall not be placed unless the ambient temperature, bridge deck surface temperature, and weather conditions comply with the requirements of Section 60-3.04B of the State Standard Specifications and the polyester concrete manufacturer's requirements. 
 
The Contractor shall furnish and place polyester concrete overlay at the locations and to the thickness shown on the Project Plans.
 
The Contractor shall protect the polyester concrete overlay from damage until the roadway is reopened to public traffic. Damage resulting from the Contractor's operations shall be repaired at the Contractor's expense.
 
Surface Smoothness
Notwithstanding the provisions of Section 51-1.01D(3)(b)(ii), “Surface Smoothness,” the Contractor shall perform the required surface smoothness testing.
 
The Contractor shall furnish all labor, equipment, and personnel necessary to perform the testing and shall demonstrate that the completed polyester concrete overlay complies with the surface smoothness requirements of Section 51-1.01D(3)(b)(ii). Test results shall be submitted to the City Engineer.
 
Areas that do not comply with the specified surface smoothness requirements shall be corrected and retested by the Contractor at no additional cost to the City.
 
The Contractor shall plan and sequence all work within the permitted lane closure hours to allow the polyester concrete overlay to satisfy the curing and opening-to-traffic requirements of Section 60-3.04B, install temporary pavement markers (TRPMs), remove traffic control devices, and fully reopen the roadway to public traffic.
 
Measurement and Payment
Polyester Concrete Overlay shall be paid for at the contract 
LUMP SUM
 price and shall include full compensation for furnishing all labor, materials, tools, equipment, testing, and incidentals necessary to complete the placement of polyester concrete overlay and perform the required surface smoothness testing as specified in the State Standard Specifications, these Special Provisions, the Project Plans, as directed by the City Engineer, and no additional compensation will be allowed therefor.

## Type "A" Asphalt Concrete 
Asphalt concrete shall be Type A and shall conform to Section 23, “Asphalt Concrete,” of the Standard Construction Specifications and these Technical Provisions.
 
Asphalt Concrete Adjacent to Curb, Gutter, and Sidewalk Type “A” asphalt concrete shall be used. The paving aggregate shall be one-half inch (1/2”) maximum, medium gradation. The paving asphalt shall be viscosity grade PG 64-10 as specified in Section 92, “Asphalts,” of the State Specifications.
 
Emulsion shall be applied to both the vertical edges of the existing pavement and to the pavement to be surfaced prior to placing new asphalt concrete. Asphaltic emulsions shall conform to “Asphaltic Emulsions Binder (Tack Coat)” of the Standard Construction Specifications and shall be included in the unit bid price for asphalt concrete and no additional compensation shall be allowed therefor.
 
Measurement and Payment
Asphalt Concrete Type A shall be paid for on a per 
TON
 basis per Section 23-11 “Measurement and Payment” of the Standard Construction Specifications. Measurement will be based on the actual tons of HMA installed as determined by the volume reported on Contractor provided truck tags. The contract unit price paid for shall include full compensation for furnishing all labor, materials, tools, equipment and incidentals and for doing all work involved in production, delivery, pre-overlay preparation, emulsion, compaction, and placement of HMA as shown on the Project Plans, as specified in these Special Provisions and as directed by the City Engineer and no additional payment shall be made.

## Adjust Utility to Grade 
As necessary due to changes in the grade of the roadway and as indicated on the Project Plans, the frames and covers of existing City and County owned utility structures shall be adjusted to grade in accordance with the provisions of Section 39-5 of the Standard Construction Specifications, these Special Provisions, the Project Plans and as directed by the City Engineer.
 
All utility structures encountered within the limits of asphalt pavement repairs and overlays shall be carefully referenced out prior to the placement of asphalt and the locations of all utility structures shall be painted on the surface immediately after paving. All drainage and sewer manhole covers within the limits of asphalt repair shall be adjusted to grade by the Contractor. Sanitary sewer manholes and drainage manholes shall be raised to grade per SASD Standard Detail MH-03.
 
Manhole openings shall be covered during the entire operation so that no debris can fall into the sewer or storm drain system. Extreme care shall be taken to prevent spilling foreign material into the drainage or sanitary sewer system.  The City Engineer will require the Contractor to immediately remove manhole covers for inspection to determine if any foreign material has fallen into the manhole. The Contractor shall be required to immediately remove all foreign material from the manhole’s interior.
 
Utility boxes encountered within the limits of construction of concrete improvements shall be inspected for structural integrity and determined acceptable for adjustment to grade. The Contractor shall coordinate with utility owner and City Engineer to determine if the utility box needs be relocated.
Contractor shall start raising iron within five (5) days of completing paving work on the street.
 
Adjusting utilities to grade must be completed, including placing paving material around and to the level of the frame and cover, by the end of the same day on which work is started.  If permanent pavement backfill cannot be completed by the end of the work day, the Contractor must place temporary paving material to the finished grade level of the frame and cover.  The Contractor must maintain the temporary paving smooth and level with the frame and cover until the permanent paving is placed.
 
Measurement and Payment
Adjust Utility to Grade shall be paid for on a per 
EACH
 basis. Measurement will be based on the actual number of utilities adjusted to grade by the Contractor as determined by actual count. The contract unit price paid for each Adjust Utility to Grade shall include full compensation for furnishing all labor, materials, tools, equipment, incidentals, and for doing all work involved in adjusting the utilities to grade including, but not limited to, manhole frames and covers, drop inlet hood and grate, sewer cleanouts, utility boxes, water valves, and monitoring wells to finished grade as shown on the Plans, as specified in the Standard Construction Specifications and these Special Provisions, and as directed by the City Engineer and no additional compensation will be allowed therefore.

## Thermoplastic Traffic Stripes 
Removal of thermoplastic traffic stripes shall conform to the provisions in Section 13-2.09, “Removal of Traffic Stripes and Pavement Markings,” of the Standard Construction Specifications, as shown on the Plans, as directed by the Engineer, and these Special Provisions. 
 
Existing pavement markers, including underlying adhesive, when no longer required for traffic lane delineation as determined by the Engineer, shall be removed and disposed of.
 
Notwithstanding Section 48-5 the Contractor shall be responsible for furnishing, installing, and maintaining temporary pavement markings on portions of the roadway shown on the Plans to receive new traffic striping or pavement markings whenever such portions are open to traffic prior to installation of the final traffic striping or pavement markings.
 
All traffic striping within the project limits shall be thermoplastic and shall be installed by the Contractor as shown on the Plans per Section 84 Markings of the State Standard Specifications and as directed by the Engineer.  
 
Contrast Striping
Traffic striping within the polyester concrete limits shall include black contrast paint applied in two coats without glass beads in accordance with Caltrans Standard Drawing A20E, “Traffic Lines – Typical Details for Contrast Striping, Option 1" and Section 84-2.03(B), “Contrast Striping,” of the State Standard Specifications and shall be installed within the limits shown on the Plans and as directed by the City Engineer.
 
Pavement Markers 
Pavement markers shall conform to Section 81-3, “Pavement Markers,” of the State Standard Specifications and shall be installed as shown on the Plans.
 
Pavement markers installed on asphalt concrete pavement shall be bonded using hot-melt bituminous adhesive or rapid-set epoxy adhesive.
 
Pavement Markers on Polyester Concrete 
Pavement markers installed on polyester concrete shall be bonded using rapid-set epoxy adhesive compatible with polyester concrete. Adhesive and surface preparation shall conform to Section 81-3 of the State Standard Specifications and the adhesive manufacturer's recommendations.
 
The Contractor shall prepare all surfaces receiving Pavement Markers such that the surfaces are clean, dry, and free of dirt, dust, debris, loose material, oil, grease, and other contaminants that may adversely affect adhesion.
 
Thermoplastics striping on Polyester Concrete
Primer or surface preparation adhesive shall be applied in accordance with Section 84-2.03B(2)(a), including the specified application rate and drying requirements.
 
The Contractor shall be responsible for providing proper surface preparation and ensuring adequate adhesion of the thermoplastic traffic striping to the polyester concrete surface.
 
Measurement and Payment
Thermoplastic traffic stripes will be measured and paid for by the 
LINEAR FOOT
 for the respective sizes and configurations shown on the Plans. The contract unit price shall include full compensation for furnishing all labor, materials, tools, equipment, and incidentals necessary to complete the work, including removal of existing traffic stripes and pavement markers; furnishing, installing, maintaining, and removing temporary pavement markings; surface preparation and cleaning; primer or surface preparation adhesive; black contrast striping where shown on the Plans; permanent thermoplastic traffic striping; and retroreflective pavement markers. No additional compensation will be allowed therefor. 
 
Surface preparation, cleaning, and application of primer or surface preparation adhesive shall be considered incidental to the thermoplastic traffic stripes, and no additional compensation will be allowed therefor.
 
Black contrast striping, where described on the Plans, shall be considered incidental to the applicable thermoplastic traffic stripe bid item.

## Development Objectives
The selected Developer will be responsible for all activities necessary to finance, design, entitle, construct, own, operate, and maintain The Ranch Affordable Housing Development in accordance with applicable laws, regulatory requirements, funding requirements, City development standards, and subsequent agreements with the City.
The Developer will be responsible for securing project financing; conducting necessary due diligence; obtaining required entitlements, permits, and approvals; retaining and managing its development team and contractors; completing design and construction; and maintaining required affordability restrictions and regulatory compliance for the applicable affordability period. The Developer shall designate a primary representative to serve as the City's point of contact during the negotiation, entitlement, and development process.
 
 
 
The City seeks a development that:
Creates at least 210 housing units for lower-income households and implements the goals and policies of the City's Housing Element.
Complements surrounding residential neighborhoods through high-quality architecture, landscaping, and site planning and complies with applicable City multifamily design guidelines and standards.
Provides safe, attractive, and functional resident amenities, community space, open space, and resident services.
Serves a mix of extremely low-, very low-, and low-income households and provides a mix of unit sizes, including family-oriented affordable rental housing.
Incorporates sustainable and resilient building practices, energy efficiency, bicycle parking, and EV charging, as appropriate.
Maximizes competitive state, federal, regional, private, and other financing while minimizing the need for City financial assistance.
Demonstrates financial feasibility and the ability to proceed efficiently through entitlement, financing, construction, occupancy, and long-term operations.
City Participation
Subject to City Council approval and applicable law, the City anticipates making the Project Site available through a land conveyance or ground lease and may provide letters of support for competitive funding applications, entitlement coordination, and other assistance as determined appropriate by the City. Local funding available for the Project is limited, and the extent to which a Proposal minimizes the need for additional City funding will be considered as part of the competitive evaluation process.
Development Requirements
The proposed development shall be affordable multifamily rental housing serving lower-income households and shall provide long-term affordability consistent with applicable regulatory and funding requirements.
The Developer shall demonstrate successful experience developing, financing, constructing, owning, managing, and maintaining comparable affordable housing.
The proposed development shall comply with applicable City development standards and design requirements, including applicable multifamily design guidelines and standards.
The Proposal shall include a conceptual design sufficient for the City to evaluate architecture, site planning, building orientation and massing, landscaping, circulation, open space, resident amenities, neighborhood compatibility, sustainability, and overall development quality.
Conceptual plans are subject to further City review and refinement. Selection does not constitute approval of the design, site plan, density, unit mix, entitlements, financing, or other development features.
The selected Developer shall be responsible for obtaining all required City and other governmental approvals necessary for the Project.

The services described herein are considered “public works” as defined by California Labor Code Section 1720 et seq. If a consultant is awarded a contract, they shall be responsible for compliance with all applicable prevailing wage laws, as well as any and all applicable state or federal wage laws for services under the Consultant’s contract.

The City of Rancho Cordova ("City") is soliciting proposals from qualified affordable housing developers for the financing, design, construction, ownership, and long-term operation of an affordable multifamily rental housing community on City-owned property located near the southeast corner of Rancho Cordova Parkway and Chrysanthy Boulevard in Rancho Cordova, California ("Project Site"), APN 067-2420-003-0000.
The City seeks to select an experienced developer with demonstrated success in delivering high-quality affordable housing developments utilizing state, federal, local, and private financing resources. The selected Developer will be expected to secure competitive funding, complete all required planning and environmental processes, construct the proposed development, and maintain the property as affordable housing for the required affordability period.
Following the evaluation and selection process, the City anticipates negotiating an Exclusive Negotiating Agreement (ENA) with the selected proposer, subject to Rancho Cordova City Council approval.

## Storm Water Pollution Control Plan
Storm Water Pollution Control work shall conform to the requirements in Section 10-4, "Erosion, Sediment, and Water Pollution Control," of the Standard Construction Specifications, and these Technical Provisions.
 
The Contractor shall minimize erosion and transport of sediments during all aspects of the project. Erosion and sediment control shall conform to the requirements of Sacramento County's "Erosion and Sediment Control Guidelines". That document is available, for a fee, from the Water Resources Division, County of Sacramento.
 
The Contractor shall be required to prepare an Erosion and Sediment Control Plan, in conformance with the "Erosion and Sediment Control Guidelines". This Plan will be subject to review and approval by the Engineer. The Plan shall be submitted to the Engineer for review at least 5 days prior to the start of construction. During the review process, the Contractor shall revise the Plan as directed by the Engineer. In no case will the Contractor be allowed to begin the clearing, grubbing, or earthwork operations without an approved Erosion and Sediment Control Plan. If the Contractor’s method fails to prevent erosion or siltation, the Contractor shall revise and adjust the control measures to provide effective control and shall be responsible for any damage resulting from erosion or siltation originating on the work site.
 
In the event that the Contractor's work is suspended due to inclement weather for a period exceeding seven (7) calendar days, all sections of curb and gutter that have been removed shall be backfilled with aggregate base to match the existing gutter grade.  Compaction shall be a minimum of ninety percent (90%) and shall be placed in such a manner as to minimize the amount of standing water in the removed gutter sections and thereby reducing water infiltration into the road base.  Driveway areas shall also be covered with trench plating.  Drop inlets downstream of curb and gutter areas that have been backfilled with aggregate base shall be protected with inlet sediment control barriers or as specified in the Contractor’s WPCP.  Upon resumption of work, the excess compacted aggregate base shall be removed with the remaining aggregate base recompacted and tested prior to curb and gutter installation.
 
Measurement and Payment

price for the Storm Water Pollution Control Plan and shall include full compensation for temporary aggregate base, trench plating, inlet protection, removal of temporary materials, recompaction, and testing required by this section shall be included in the Lump Sum price paid for Storm Water Pollution Control Plan, and no additional compensation will be made therefor.

## Tree Root Control Barrier
Removal of tree roots shall conform to Section 15, “Clearing and Grubbing,” of the Standard Construction Specifications, these Technical Provisions, and as directed by the Engineer. The Contractor shall remove tree roots where noted in the “Tree Root Trim” section of the “Locations List” found in these Technical Provisions.
 
Roots larger than 2 inches in diameter must be reviewed by the City arborist prior to cutting and removal. The contractor shall be required to notify the City arborist 48 hours prior to any work in the vicinity of tree roots larger than 2" in diameter.
 
Tree roots shall be neatly trimmed by means of a root cutter, and roots greater than two inches in diameter shall be coated with a heavy coat of an approved tree seal compound approved by the Engineer.
 
Roots shall be removed in such a manner as not to injure adjacent standing trees, plants, and other landscaping which are to be preserved. Hand digging within root zone is required in order to expose roots with minimal damage. The root zone is defined as the area of ground within the dripline of the tree and extending to a depth of 24 inches. Tree roots over 12 inches below grade may be left in place. If severing of roots cannot be avoided, a sharp tool such as pruning shears, loppers, or a handsaw shall be used to produce a clean cut in order to reduce wound size and encourage healing. The Inspector shall observe all root trimming activities. A maximum of 25% of the root mass may be trimmed and treated with root barrier.
 
Aggregate base shall be compacted around remaining roots to required density.

Fugitive dust, sometimes referred to as windblown dust or PM10, would be the primary short-term construction impact, which may be generated during excavation, grading and hauling activities. However, both fugitive dust and construction equipment exhaust emissions would be temporary and transitory in nature. Standard BMP’s to contain fugitive dust should effectively reduce and control emission impacts during construction.

## DISADVANTAGED BUSINESS ENTERPRISES (DBE)
The contractor, subrecipient or subcontractor shall take necessary and reasonable steps to ensure that DBEs have opportunity to participate in the contract (49 CFR 26). To ensure equal participation of DBEs provided in 49 CFR 26.5, the Agency shows a contract goal for DBEs. The prime contractor shall make work available to DBEs and select work parts consistent with available DBE subcontractors and suppliers.
The prime contractor shall meet the DBE goal shown elsewhere in these special provisions or demonstrate that they made adequate Good Faith Efforts (GFE) to meet this goal. An adequate GFE means that the bidder must show that it took all necessary and reasonable steps to achieve a DBE goal that, by their scope, intensity, and appropriateness to the objective, could reasonably be expected to meet the DBE goal.
If the DBE goal is not met, the contractor needs to complete and submit the DBE GFE documentation as described in Local Assistance Procedures Manual (LAPM) Chapter 9, Section 9.8 within 5 (five) days of bid opening.
It is the prime contractor’s responsibility to verify that the DBE firm is certified as a DBE on the date of bid opening by using the California Unified Certification Program (CUCP) database and possesses the most specific available North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and Work Code applicable to the type of work the firm will perform on the contract. Additionally, the prime contractor is responsible to document this verification by printing out the CUCP data for each DBE firm. A list of DBEs certified by the CUCP can be found at: 
https://dot.ca.gov/programs/civil-rights/dbe-search
.
DBE participation will only count toward the California Department of Transportation’s federally mandated statewide overall DBE goal if the DBE performs a commercially useful function under 49 CFR 26.55.
Credit for materials or supplies the prime contractor purchases from DBEs counts towards the goal in the following manner:
100 percent counts if the materials or supplies are obtained from a DBE manufacturer.
60 percent counts if the materials or supplies are obtained from a DBE regular dealer.
Only fees, commissions, and charges for assistance in the procurement and delivery of materials or supplies count if obtained from a DBE that is neither a manufacturer nor regular dealer. 49 CFR 26.55 defines "manufacturer" and "regular dealer."
The prime contractor receives credit towards the goal if they employ a DBE trucking company that performs a commercially useful function as defined in 49 CFR 26.55(d) as follows:
The DBE must be responsible for the management and supervision of the entire trucking operation for which it is responsible on a particular contract, and there cannot be a contrived arrangement for the purpose of meeting DBE goals.
The DBE must itself own and operate at least one fully licensed, insured, and operational truck used on the contract.
The DBE receives credit for the total value of the transportation services it provides on the Contract using trucks it owns, insures, and operates using drivers it employs.
The DBE may lease trucks from another DBE firm, including an owner-operator who is certified as a DBE. The DBE who leases trucks from another DBE receives credit for the total value of the transportation services the lessee DBE provides on the Contract.
The DBE may also lease trucks from a non-DBE firm, including from an owner-operator. The DBE that leases trucks equipped with drivers from a non-DBE is entitled to credit for the total value of transportation services provided by non-DBE leased trucks equipped with drivers not to exceed the value of transportation services on the contract provided by DBE-owned trucks or leased trucks with DBE employee drivers. Additional participation by non-DBE owned trucks equipped with drivers receives credit only for the fee or commission it receives as a result of the lease arrangement.
The DBE may lease trucks without drivers from a non-DBE truck leasing company. If the DBE leases trucks from a non-DBE truck leasing company and uses its own employees as drivers, it is entitled to credit for the total value of these hauling services.
A lease must indicate that the DBE has exclusive use of and control over the truck. This does not preclude the leased truck from working for others during the term of the lease with the consent of the DBE, so long as the lease gives the DBE absolute priority for use of the leased truck. Leased trucks must display the name and identification number of the DBE.

Prompt Progress Payment
In accordance with California Business and Professions Code section 7108.5, the prime contractor or subcontractor shall pay to any subcontractor, not later than seven days after receipt of each progress payment, unless otherwise agreed to in writing, the respective amounts allowed the contractor on account of the work performed by the subcontractors, to the extent of each subcontractor’s interest therein. In the event that there is a good faith dispute over all or any portion of the amount due on a progress payment from the prime contractor or subcontractor to a subcontractor, the prime contractor or subcontractor may withhold no more than 150 percent of the disputed amount. Any violation of this requirement shall constitute a cause for disciplinary action and shall subject the licensee to a penalty, payable to the subcontractor, of 2 percent of the amount due per month for every month that payment is not made.
In any action for the collection of funds wrongfully withheld, the prevailing party shall be entitled to his or her attorney’s fees and costs. The sanctions authorized under this requirement shall be separate from, and in addition to, all other remedies, either civil, administrative, or criminal. This clause applies to both DBE and non-DBE subcontractors.
Prompt Payment of Withheld Funds to Subcontractors
The Agency may hold retainage from the prime contractor and shall make prompt and regular incremental acceptances of portions, as determined by the Agency, of the contract work, and pay retainage to the prime contractor based on these acceptances. The Agency shall designate one of the methods below in the contract to ensure prompt and full payment of any retainage kept by the prime contractor or subcontractor to a subcontractor. The Agency shall include either Method 1, Method 2, or Method 3 below and delete the other two.
Method 1: 
No retainage will be held by the Agency from progress payments due to the prime contractor. Prime contractors and subcontractors are prohibited from holding retainage from subcontractors. Any delay or postponement of payment may take place only for good cause and with the Agency’s prior written approval. Any violation of these provisions shall subject the violating contractor or subcontractor to the penalties, sanctions, and other remedies specified in Section 7108.5 of the California Business and Professions Code and Section 10262 of the California Public Contract Code. This requirement shall not be construed to limit or impair any contractual, administrative or judicial remedies, otherwise available to the contractor or subcontractor in the event of a dispute involving late payment or nonpayment by the contractor, deficient subcontractor performance and/or noncompliance by a subcontractor. This clause applies to both DBE and non-DBE subcontractors.
Method 2:
 No retainage will be held by the Agency from progress payments due to the prime contractor. Any retainage kept by the prime contractor or by a subcontractor must be paid in full to the earning subcontractor within seven (7) days after the subcontractor’s work is satisfactorily completed. Any delay or postponement of payment may take place only for good cause and with the Agency’s prior written approval. Any violation of these provisions shall subject the violating contractor or subcontractor to the penalties, sanctions, and remedies specified in Section 7108.5 of the California Business and Professions Code and Section 10262 of the California Public Contract Code. This requirement shall not be construed to limit or impair any contractual, administrative or judicial remedies, otherwise available to the contractor or subcontractor in the event of a dispute involving late payment or nonpayment by the contractor, deficient subcontractor performance and/or noncompliance by a subcontractor. This clause applies to both DBE and non-DBE subcontractors.
Method 3:
 The Agency shall hold retainage from the prime contractor and shall make prompt and regular incremental acceptances of portions, as determined by the Agency of the contract work and pay retainage to the prime contractor based on these acceptances. The prime contractor or subcontractor shall return all monies withheld in retention from all subcontractors within seven (7) days after receiving payment for work satisfactorily completed and accepted including incremental acceptances of portions of the contract work by the Agency. Any delay or postponement of payment may take place only for good cause and with the Agency’s prior written approval. Any violation of these provisions shall subject the violating prime contractor or subcontractor to the penalties, sanctions, and other remedies specified in Section 7108.5 of the California Business and Professions Code and Section 10262 of the California Public Contract Code. This requirement shall not be construed to limit or impair any contractual, administrative or judicial remedies otherwise available to the contractor or subcontractor in the event of a dispute involving late payment or nonpayment by the contractor; deficient subcontractor performance and/or noncompliance by a subcontractor. This clause applies to both DBE and non-DBE subcontractors.
Any violation of these provisions of Prompt Progress Payment and Prompt Payment of Withheld Funds to Subcontractors shall subject the violating prime contractor or subcontractor to the penalties, sanctions and other remedies specified therein. These requirements shall not be construed to limit or impair any contractual, administrative, or judicial remedies otherwise available to the prime contractor or subcontractor in the event of a dispute involving late payment or nonpayment by the prime contractor, deficient subcontract performance, or noncompliance by a subcontractor.

Listed DBE fails or refuses to execute a written contract based on plans and specifications for the project.
The Local Agency stipulated that a bond is a condition of executing the subcontract and the listed DBE fails to meet the Local Agency’s bond requirements.
Work requires a contractor's license and listed DBE does not have a valid license under Contractors License Law, or is not properly registered with the California Department of Industrial Relations as a public works contractor.
Listed DBE fails or refuses to perform the work or furnish the listed materials (failing or refusing to perform is not an allowable reason to remove a DBE if the failure or refusal is a result of bad faith or discrimination).
Listed DBE's work is unsatisfactory and not in compliance with the contract.
Listed DBE is ineligible to work on the project because of suspension or debarment.
Listed DBE becomes bankrupt or insolvent or exhibits credit unworthiness.
Listed DBE voluntarily withdraws with written notice from the Contract
Listed DBE is ineligible to receive credit for the type of work required.
Listed DBE owner dies or becomes disabled resulting in the inability to perform the work on the Contract.
The Agency determines other documented good cause.

The DBE's response to Contractor’s written notice, if received. If a written response was not provided, provide a statement to that effect.

Commercially Useful Function
DBEs must perform a commercially useful function (CUF) under 49 CFR 26.55 when performing work or supplying materials listed on the DBE Commitment form. The DBE value of work will only count toward the DBE commitment if the DBE performs a CUF. A DBE performs a CUF when it is responsible for execution of the work on the contract and is carrying out its responsibilities by actually performing, managing, and supervising the work involved. If a DBE does not perform or exercise responsibility for at least 30% of the total cost of its contract with its own work force, or the DBE subcontracts a greater portion of the work of a contract than would be expected on the basis of normal industry practice for the type of work involved, it will be presumed that the DBE is not performing a CUF. Additionally, the DBE must also be responsible, with respect to materials and supplies used on the contract, for negotiating price, determining quality and quantity, ordering the material and installing (where applicable), and paying for the material itself.
The Contractor must perform CUF evaluation for each DBE company working on a federal-aid contract, with or without a DBE goal. Perform a CUF evaluation at the beginning of the DBE’s work, and continue to monitor the performance of CUF for the duration of the project.
The Contractor must provide written notification to the AGENCY at least 15 days in advance of each DBE's initial performance of work or supplying materials for the Contract. The notification must include the DBE's name, work the DBE will perform on the contract, and the location, date, and time of where their work will take place.
Within 10 (ten) days of a DBE initially performing work or supplying materials on the contract, the Contractor shall submit to the LPA the initial evaluation and validation of DBE performance of a CUF using the LAPM 9-J: Disadvantaged Business Enterprise Commercially Useful Function Evaluation. Include the following information with the submittal:
Subcontract agreement with the DBE
Purchase orders
Bills of lading
Invoices
Proof of payment
The Contractor must monitor all DBE’s performance of CUF by conducting quarterly evaluations and validations throughout their duration of work on the contract using the LAPM 9-J: DBE Commercially Useful Function Evaluation. The Contractor must submit to the AGENCY these quarterly evaluations and validations by the 5th of the month for the previous three (3) months of work.
The Contractor must notify the AGENCY immediately if the Contractor believes the DBE may not be performing a CUF.
The AGENCY will verify DBEs performance of CUF by reviewing the initial and quarterly submissions of LAPM 9-J: DBE Commercially Useful Function Evaluation, submitted supporting information, field observations, and through any additional AGENCY evaluations. The AGENCY must evaluate DBEs and their CUF performance throughout the duration of a Contract. The AGENCY will provide written notice to Contractor and DBE at least two (2) business days prior to any evaluation. The Contractor and DBE must participate in the evaluation. Upon completing the evaluation, the AGENCY must share the evaluation results with the Contractor and DBE. An evaluation could include items that must be remedied upon receipt. If the AGENCY determines the DBE is not performing a CUF the Contractor must suspend performance of the noncompliant work.
The Contractor and DBEs must submit any additional CUF related records and documents within five (5) business days of AGENCY’s request such as:
Proof of ownership or lease and rental agreements for equipment
Tax records
Employee rosters
Certified payroll records
Inventory rosters
Failure to submit required DBE Commercially Useful Function Evaluation forms or requested records and documents can result in withholding of payment for the value of work completed by the DBE.
If the Contractor and/or the AGENCY determine that a listed DBE is not performing a CUF in performance of their DBE committed work, immediately suspend performance of the noncompliant portion of the work. The AGENCY may deny payment for the noncompliant portion of the work. The AGENCY will ask the Contractor to submit a corrective action plan (CAP) to the AGENCY within five (5) days of the noncompliant CUF determination. The CAP must identify how the Contractor will correct the noncompliance findings for the remaining portion of the DBE's work. The AGENCY has five (5) days to review the CAP in conjunction with the prime contractor’s review. The Contractor must implement the CAP within five (5) days of the AGENCY's approval. The AGENCY will then authorize the prior noncompliant portion of work for the DBE's committed work.
If corrective actions cannot be accomplished to ensure the DBE performs a CUF on the Contract, then the Contractor may have good cause to request termination of the DBE.
Use of Joint Checks
A joint check may be used between the Contractor or lower-tier subcontractor and a DBE subcontractor purchasing materials from a material supplier if the contractor obtains prior approval from the LPA for the proposed use of joint check upon submittal of the LAPM 9-K: DLA Disadvantaged Business Enterprises (DBE) Joint Check Agreement Request form.
