## Post Project Report, Framework & Data Collection
The El Molino Avenue Demonstration Project will use both quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods including crash data, traffic volumes and speeds, pedestrian and bicyclist activity, and community feedback to assess the benefits of the project and inform the in-process development of the Citywide Active Transportation Plan. The data collection for the post project report will have a similar approach to the baseline condition report. Traffic counts shall be collected again for El Molino Avenue and parallel street. A core goal is to familiarize the Pasadena community with demonstration projects and quick‑build strategies that can deliver low‑cost, temporary, high‑impact safety improvements and guide future community engagement on similar projects. To support long‑term implementation, the Consultant shall develop a user‑friendly reporting framework that enables City staff to independently prepare post‑implementation evaluation reports without ongoing consultant assistance. This framework will provide standardized narrative sections, data‑input guidance, mapping and graphic templates, performance measures, before‑and‑after analysis methods, community feedback summaries, and documentation steps needed to meet current and future funding requirements, ensuring consistent, evidence‑based planning for permanent safety improvements. Data from pre‑and post‑project community surveys shall be incorporated into the evaluation framework.
 
DELIVERABLE:
Data Collection – Traffic Counts (Similar to Baseline Condition Report):
Eight (8) multimodal roadway segment counts: (4 on El Molino Avenue and 4 on two parallel streets), collected on a representative weekday and weekend day to capture all modes as described above.
Four (4) intersection turning movement counts collected during AM and PM peak hours on a representative weekday and weekend day to capture all modes as described above.
Two (2) speed surveys on El Molino Avenue where speeding concerns identified

## CONTRACT WORK HOURS AND SAFETY STANDARDS ACT
REQUIRED FOR FEDERALLY FUNDED AGREEMENTS IN EXCESS OF $100,000 AND INVOLVES THE EMPLOYMENT OF MECHANICS OR LABORERS. The Contractor shall comply with 40 U.S.C. §§ 3702 and 3704, as supplemented by Department of Labor regulations at 29 C.F.R. Part 5. See 2 C.F.R. Part 200, Appendix II(E). Under 40 U.S.C. § 3702, each contractor must be required to compute the wages of every mechanic and laborer on the basis of a standard work week of 40 hours. Work in excess of the standard workweek is permissible provided that the worker is compensated at a rate of not less than one and a half times the basic rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of 40 hours in the work week. Further, no laborer or mechanic must be required to work in surroundings or under working conditions which are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous. Overtime requirements. No contractor or subcontractor contracting for any part of the contract work which may require or involve the employment of laborers or mechanics shall require or permit any such laborer or mechanic in any workweek in which he or she is employed on such work to work in excess of forty hours in such workweek unless such laborer or mechanic receives compensation at a rate not less than one and one-half times the basic rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of forty hours in such workweek. Violation; liability for unpaid wages; liquidated damages. In the event of any violation of the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section the contractor and any subcontractor responsible therefor shall be liable for the unpaid wages. In addition, such contractor and subcontractor shall be liable to the United States (in the case of work done under contract for the District of Columbia or a territory, to such District or to such territory), for liquidated damages. Such liquidated damages shall be computed with respect to each individual laborer or mechanic, including watchmen and guards, employed in violation of the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section, in the sum of $27 for each calendar day on which such individual was required or permitted to work in excess of the standard workweek of forty hours without payment of the overtime wages required by the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section. SUMMARY: 
The Office of Management and Budget is revising the OMB Guidance for Grants and Agreements. The revisions are limited in scope to support implementation of the Build America, Buy America Act provisions of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and to clarify existing provisions related to domestic preferences. These revisions provide further guidance on implementing the statutory requirements and improve Federal financial assistance management and transparency. 
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 
Executive Summary 
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) is revising its guidance in title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations (2 CFR) to add a new part 184 and revise 2 CFR 200.322. The revisions implement the requirement for the Director of OMB to issue guidance to the head of each Federal agency to assist in the implementation of the requirements of the Build America, Buy America Act (BABA), Public Law 117-58, 135 Stat. 429, 70901-70927, Nov. 15, 2021. As required by BABA, the new part 184 of 2 CFR provides clear and consistent guidance to Federal agencies about how to apply the domestic content procurement preference (Buy This document is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on 08/23/2023 and available online at federalregister.gov/d/2023-17724, and on govinfo.gov America or BABA preference) as set forth in BABA to Federal awards for infrastructure projects. See BABA 70915. For example, the new part 184 includes definitions for key terms, including iron or steel products, manufactured products, construction materials, and materials identified in section 70917(c) (section 70917(c) materials) of BABA. These definitions provide a common system for Federal agencies to distinguish between the product categories established under the statutory text in BABA. The new part also offers standards that define “all manufacturing processes” in the case of construction materials. The new part 184 also includes guidance for determining the cost of components of manufactured products. The part 184 text uses a modified version of the “cost of components” test found in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) at 48 CFR 25.003, which is used for Federal procurement. Using this approach for determining the cost of components of manufactured products in the context of Federal financial assistance aims to provide a consistent approach for industry, with only minor modifications which are explained in this document. The new part 184 also includes guidance on proposing and issuing Buy America waivers. For example, based on the statutory text of BABA, it restates the circumstances under which a waiver may be justified. The new part also includes guidance on the type of process that a Federal agency should implement to allow recipients to request waivers, including the process a Federal agency should follow in issuing proposed and final waivers. The revised provision in 2 CFR part 200 specifies that Federal agencies providing Federal financial assistance for infrastructure projects must implement the Buy America preferences set forth in 2 CFR part 184, as required under section 70914(a) BABA, as of the effective date of the guidance, unless specified otherwise.

## Public Contract Claims Procedure
PUBLIC CONTRACT CODE SECTION 9204 PUBLIC WORKS CLAIMS PROCEDURE
AB 626, approved by the Governor on September 29, 2016, created a new Public Contract Code Section 9204, which specifies new procedural requirements for claims submitted by a contractor on any public works project. These new requirements contain burdens for both private contractors and public entities and are specifically made applicable to charter cities.
For this legislation, a “public works project” is defined as “the erection, construction, alteration, repair, or improvement of any public structure, building, road, or other public improvement of any kind.” This definition is not as broad as in the Prevailing Wage Law.
A “claim” is defined as “a separate demand by a contractor sent by registered mail or certified mail with return receipt requested…” and is limited to three types of contract disputes:
1. “A time extension…for relief from damages or penalties for delay assessed by a public entity….”
2. “Payment by the public entity of money or damages arising from work done by, or on behalf of, the contractor pursuant to the contract for a public works project and payment for which is not otherwise expressly provided or to which the claimant is not otherwise entitled”, and/or
3. “Payment of an amount that is disputed by the public entity.”
Upon receipt of a claim, a public entity must "conduct a reasonable review" and provide a written statement to the contractor within 45 days of receipt of the claim. Failure of a public entity to respond to a claim within the time periods described in Section 9204 "shall result in the claim being deemed rejected in its entirety."
For any undisputed portion of a claim, a public entity must make payment within 60 days of the public entity's issuance of the written statement.
If the contractor disputes the public entity's written statement, or if the public entity fails to respond, the contractor may demand "an informal conference to meet and confer for settlement of the issues in dispute." The public entity must schedule the meet and confer conference within 30 days of the demand.
Within 10 business days following the meet and confer conference, the public entity must provide a written statement identifying the portion of the claim that remains in dispute.
Any payment due on an undisputed portion of the claim must be made within 60 days of the meet and confer conference. Amounts not paid in a timely manner shall bear interest at 7 percent per year.
After the meet and confer conference, any disputed portion of the claim "shall be submitted to non-binding mediation." If mediation fails to resolve the dispute, the parts of the claim that remain in dispute shall be subject to applicable procedures outside Section 9204 (statutory and contractual).
The full text of this new legislation is set forth below:
THE PEOPLE OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA DO ENACT AS FOLLOWS:
SECTION 1.
Section 9204 is added to the Public Contract Code, to read:
9204.
(a) The Legislature finds and declares that it is in the best interests of the state and its citizens to ensure that all construction business performed on a public works project in the state that is complete and not in dispute is paid in full and in a timely manner.
(b) Notwithstanding any other law, including, but not limited to, Article 7.1 (commencing with Section 10240) of Chapter 1 of Part 2, Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 19100) of Part 2, and Article 1.5 (commencing with Section 20104) of Chapter 1 of Part 3, this section shall apply to any claim by a contractor in connection with a public works project.
(c) For purposes of this section:
(1) “Claim” means a separate demand by a contractor sent by registered mail or certified mail with return receipt requested, for one or more of the following:
(A) A time extension, including, without limitation, for relief from damages or penalties for delay assessed by a public entity under a contract for a public works project.
(B) Payment by the public entity of money or damages arising from work done by, or on behalf of, the contractor pursuant to the contract for a public works project and payment for which is not otherwise expressly provided or to which the claimant is not otherwise entitled.
(C) Payment of an amount that is disputed by the public entity.
(2) “Contractor” means any type of contractor within the meaning of Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code who has entered into a direct contract with a public entity for a public works project.
(3) (A) “Public entity” means, without limitation, except as provided in subparagraph (B), a state agency, department, office, division, bureau, board, or commission, the California State University, the University of California, a city, including a charter city, county, including a charter county, city and county, including a charter city and county, district, special district, public authority, political subdivision, public corporation, or nonprofit transit corporation wholly owned by a public agency and formed to carry out the purposes of the public agency.
(B) “Public entity” shall not include the following:
The Department of Water Resources as to any project under the jurisdiction of that department.
The Department of Transportation as to any project under the jurisdiction of that department.
The Department of Parks and Recreation as to any project under the jurisdiction of that department.
The Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation with respect to any project under its jurisdiction pursuant to Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 7000) of Title 7 of Part 3 of the Penal Code.
The Military Department as to any project under the jurisdiction of that department.
The Department of General Services as to all other projects.
The High-Speed Rail Authority.
(4) “Public works project” means the erection, construction, alteration, repair, or improvement of any public structure, building, road, or other public improvement of any kind.
(5) “Subcontractor” means any type of contractor within the meaning of Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code who either is in direct contract with a contractor or is a lower tier subcontractor.
(d) (1) (A) Upon receipt of a claim pursuant to this section, the public entity to which the claim applies shall conduct a reasonable review of the claim and, within a period not to exceed 45 days, shall provide the claimant a written statement identifying what portion of the claim is disputed and what portion is undisputed. Upon receipt of a claim, a public entity and a contractor may, by mutual agreement, extend the time period provided in this subdivision.
(B) The claimant shall furnish reasonable documentation to support the claim.
(C) If the public entity needs approval from its governing body to provide the claimant a written statement identifying the disputed portion and the undisputed portion of the claim, and the governing body does not meet within the 45 days or within the mutually agreed to extension of time following receipt of a claim sent by registered mail or certified mail, return receipt requested, the public entity shall have up to three days following the next duly publicly noticed meeting of the governing body after the 45-day period, or extension, expires to provide the claimant a written statement identifying the disputed portion and the undisputed portion.
(D) Any payment due on an undisputed portion of the claim shall be processed and made within 60 days after the public entity issues its written statement. If the public entity fails to issue a written statement, paragraph (3) shall apply.
(2) (A) If the claimant disputes the public entity’s written response, or if the public entity fails to respond to a claim issued pursuant to this section within the time prescribed, the claimant may demand in writing an informal conference to meet and confer for settlement of the issues in dispute. Upon receipt of a demand in writing sent by registered mail or certified mail, return receipt requested, the public entity shall schedule a meet and confer conference within 30 days for settlement of the dispute.
(B) Within 10 business days following the conclusion of the meet and confer conference, if the claim or any portion of the claim remains in dispute, the public entity shall provide the claimant a written statement identifying the portion of the claim that remains in dispute and the portion that is undisputed. Any payment due on an undisputed portion of the claim shall be processed and made within 60 days after the public entity issues its written statement. Any disputed portion of the claim, as identified by the contractor in writing, shall be submitted to nonbinding mediation, with the public entity and the claimant sharing the associated costs equally. The public entity and claimant shall mutually agree to a mediator within 10 business days after the disputed portion of the claim has been identified in writing. If the parties cannot agree upon a mediator, each party shall select a mediator and those mediators shall select a qualified neutral third party to mediate with regard to the disputed portion of the claim. Each party shall bear the fees and costs charged by its respective mediator in connection with the selection of the neutral mediator. If mediation is unsuccessful, the parts of the claim remaining in dispute shall be subject to applicable procedures outside this section.
(C) For purposes of this section, mediation includes any nonbinding process, including, but not limited to, neutral evaluation or a dispute review board, in which an independent third party or board assists the parties in dispute resolution through negotiation or by issuance of an evaluation. Any mediation utilized shall conform to the timeframes in this section.
(D) Unless otherwise agreed to by the public entity and the contractor in writing, the mediation conducted pursuant to this section shall excuse any further obligation under Section 20104.4 to mediate after litigation has been commenced.
(E) This section does not preclude a public entity from requiring arbitration of disputes under private arbitration or the Public Works Contract Arbitration Program, if mediation under this section does not resolve the parties’ dispute.
(3) Failure by the public entity to respond to a claim from a contractor within the time periods described in this subdivision or to otherwise meet the time requirements of this section shall result in the claim being deemed rejected in its entirety. A claim that is denied by reason of the public entity’s failure to have responded to a claim, or its failure to otherwise meet the time requirements of this section, shall not constitute an adverse finding with regard to the merits of the claim or the responsibility or qualifications of the claimant.
(4) Amounts not paid in a timely manner as required by this section shall bear interest at 7 percent per annum.
(5) If a subcontractor or a lower tier subcontractor lacks legal standing to assert a claim against a public entity because privity of contract does not exist, the contractor may present to the public entity a claim on behalf of a subcontractor or lower tier subcontractor. A subcontractor may request in writing, either on his or her own behalf or on behalf of a lower tier subcontractor, that the contractor present a claim for work which was performed by the subcontractor or by a lower tier subcontractor on behalf of the subcontractor. The subcontractor requesting that the claim be presented to the public entity shall furnish reasonable documentation to support the claim. Within 45 days of receipt of this written request, the contractor shall notify the subcontractor in writing as to whether the contractor presented the claim to the public entity and, if the original contractor did not present the claim, provide the subcontractor with a statement of the reasons for not having done so.
(e) The text of this section or a summary of it shall be set forth in the plans or specifications for any public works project that may give rise to a claim under this section.
(f) A waiver of the rights granted by this section is void and contrary to public policy, provided, however, that (1) upon receipt of a claim, the parties may mutually agree to waive, in writing, mediation and proceed directly to the commencement of a civil action or binding arbitration, as applicable; and (2) a public entity may prescribe reasonable change order, claim, and dispute resolution procedures and requirements in addition to the provisions of this section, so long as the contractual provisions do not conflict with or otherwise impair the timeframes and procedures set forth in this section.
(g) This section applies to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2017.
(h) Nothing in this section shall impose liability upon a public entity that makes loans or grants available through a competitive application process, for the failure of an awardee to meet its contractual obligations.
(i) This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2027, and as of that date is repealed, unless a later enacted statute that is enacted before January 1, 2027, deletes or extends that date.
(Amended by Stats. 2019, Ch. 489, Sec. 1. (AB 456) Effective January 1, 2020. Repealed as of January 1, 2027, by its own provisions.)

11.   CONTRACT WORK HOURS AND SAFETY STANDARDS ACT
REQUIRED FOR FEDERALLY FUNDED AGREEMENTS IN EXCESS OF $100,000 AND INVOLVES THE EMPLOYMENT OF MECHANICS OR LABORERS.
 
The Contractor shall comply with 40 U.S.C. §§ 3702 and 3704, as supplemented by Department of Labor regulations at 29 C.F.R. Part 5. See 2 C.F.R. Part 200, Appendix II(E). Under 40 U.S.C. § 3702, each contractor must be required to compute the wages of every mechanic and laborer on the basis of a standard work week of 40 hours. Work in excess of the standard workweek is permissible provided that the worker is compensated at a rate of not less than one and a half times the basic rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of 40 hours in the work week. Further, no laborer or mechanic must be required to work in surroundings or under working conditions which are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous.
 
1. Overtime requirements. No contractor or subcontractor contracting for any part of the contract work which may require or involve the employment of laborers or mechanics shall require or permit any such laborer or mechanic in any workweek in which he or she is employed on such work to work in excess of forty hours in such workweek unless such laborer or mechanic receives compensation at a rate not less than one and one-half times the basic rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of forty hours in such workweek.
2. Violation; liability for unpaid wages; liquidated damages. In the event of any violation of the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section the contractor and any subcontractor responsible therefor shall be liable for the unpaid wages. In addition, such contractor and subcontractor shall be liable to the United States (in the case of work done under contract for the District of Columbia or a territory, to such District or to such territory), for liquidated damages. Such liquidated damages shall be computed with respect to each individual laborer or mechanic, including watchmen and guards, employed in violation of the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section, in the sum of $27 for each calendar day on which such individual was required or permitted to work in excess of the standard workweek of forty hours without payment of the overtime wages required by the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section.
3. Withholding for unpaid wages and liquidated damages. The (City of Pasadena) shall upon its own action or upon written request of an authorized representative of the Department of Labor withhold or cause to be withheld, from any moneys payable on account of work performed by the contractor or subcontractor under any such contract or any other Federal contract with the same prime contractor, or any other federally-assisted contract subject to the Contract Work
 
Hours and Safety Standards Act, which is held by the same prime contractor, such sums as may be determined to be necessary to satisfy any liabilities of such contractor or subcontractor for unpaid wages and liquidated damages as provided in the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(2) of this section.
4. Subcontracts. The contractor or subcontractor shall insert in any subcontracts the clauses set forth in paragraph (b)(1) through (4) of this section and also a clause requiring the subcontractors to include these clauses in any lower tier subcontracts. The prime contractor shall be responsible for compliance by any subcontractor or lower tier subcontractor with the clauses set forth in paragraphs (b)(1) through (4) of this section.

12.   Copyright and Data Rights
An NFE is required by 2 C.F.R. § 200.315 to provide certain licenses with respect to copyright and data to the federal awarding agency. 2 C.F.R. § 200.315(b) provides to the federal awarding agency “a royalty-free, nonexclusive and irrevocable right to reproduce, publish, or otherwise use [any work that is subject to copyright] for federal purposes, and to authorize others to do so.” 2 C.F.R. § 200.315(d) provides to the federal government the rights to “obtain, reproduce, publish, or otherwise use” data produced under a federal award and to authorize others to do the same.
 
Applicability
When an NFE enters into a contract requiring a contractor or subcontractor to produce copyrightable subject matter and/or data for the NFE under the award, the NFE should include appropriate copyright and data licenses to meet its obligations under 2 C.F.R. § 200.315(b) and (d), respectively. Work that is subject to copyright, or copyrightable subject matter, includes any written reports or literary works, software and/or source code, music, choreography, pictures or images, graphics, sculptures, videos, motion pictures or other audiovisual works, sound and/or video recordings, and architectural works.

For data required by the contract but not first produced in the performance of this contract, the Contractor will identify such data and grant to the (City of Pasadena) or acquires on its behalf a license of the same scope as for data first produced in the performance of this contract. Data, as used herein, shall include any work subject to copyright under 17 U.S.C. § 102, for example, any written reports or literary works, software and/or source code, music, choreography, pictures or images, graphics, sculptures, videos, motion pictures or other audiovisual works, sound and/or video recordings, and architectural works. Upon or before the completion of this contract, the Contractor will deliver to the (City of Pasadena) data first produced in the performance of this contract and data required by the contract but not first produced in the performance of this contract in formats acceptable by the (City of Pasadena).”

## Background / Overview
PWP's power delivery system includes 12 substations, 37 subtransmission lines operating at 34 kV, and 118 distribution feeders operating at 17 kV and 4 kV. The system includes 54 substation transformers and approximately 300 circuit breakers.
About 75% of PWP's lines are installed underground in conduits. The subtransmission system ties the supply of power from the east and west ends of Pasadena to distribution substations throughout the city. PWP-owned generation consists of five generators totaling approximately 200 MW. PWP's contractual import capacity is 336 MW, delivered over two 230-kV lines that tie PWP to the California Independent System Operator ("CAISO") system through Southern California Edison ("SCE").
The PWP system design is robust, but aging infrastructure is a substantial concern, and the system will face capacity and reliability challenges as the City of Pasadena grows and changes. PWP is considering a number of projects to ensure the system continues to serve the community reliably. Engineering services are needed to supplement PWP engineering resources in completing these projects.

## Scope of Work 1: Receiving Station and Substation Design
Complete design of new receiving station and substation facilities and modifications to existing facilities. Voltage ratings range from 4.16 kV to 230 kV. Consultant shall have at least five (5) years of experience designing new, or modifying existing, electric utility receiving stations and substations in compliance with applicable IEEE, ANSI, NESC, NEC, California Building Code, and other applicable industry standards. Consultant shall have completed at least five (5) similar projects within the past five (5) years. Consultant staff shall include electrical, civil, structural, and geotechnical engineering personnel, as applicable to the work being performed. Professional engineering services requiring registration shall be performed under the responsible charge of engineers registered in the State of California. All work shall comply with PWP's applicable design criteria, standards, operating practices, and equipment requirements. Receiving station and substation engineering design services may include, but are not limited to:
New Receiving Stations and Substations
 – Site development and complete electrical, civil, structural, geotechnical, protection, control, automation, communications, and auxiliary system design for new facilities, including preparation of plans, equipment specifications, material lists, cost estimates, construction packages, and construction support.
Station Expansion and Modification
 – Design modifications to existing receiving stations and substations, including addition or replacement of transformers, circuit breakers, switchgear, buses, disconnect switches, instrument transformers, surge arresters, grounding equipment, capacitor banks, station service equipment, control buildings, and associated facilities.
Power Transformer Engineering
 – Preparation and review of power transformer technical specifications, equipment ratings, impedance requirements, LTC requirements, auxiliary equipment, monitoring systems, protection requirements, foundation requirements, seismic requirements, factory drawings, factory testing, field installation, testing, and commissioning requirements.
High and Medium Voltage Equipment
 – Engineering and specification of circuit breakers, disconnect switches, switchgear, bus systems, instrument transformers, surge arresters, grounding transformers, station service transformers, capacitor banks, and other station equipment. Evaluate equipment ratings including voltage, continuous current, short circuit withstand and interrupting capability, insulation level, seismic qualification, and physical clearances.
Protection and Control Systems
 – Design protective relaying and control schemes for transmission lines, subtransmission lines, transformers, buses, feeders, capacitor banks, reactors, generators, and other station equipment. Prepare and modify single-line diagrams, three-line diagrams, AC and DC schematics, wiring diagrams, elementary diagrams, interconnection diagrams, panel drawings, conduit and cable schedules, and relay/control panel designs.
Protection System Studies
 – Perform short circuit, protective device coordination, relay application and settings, current transformer performance, breaker duty, and related protection studies necessary for equipment application and station protection design.
Metering
 – Design revenue, interchange, operational, and station metering systems, including instrument transformer application, meter panels, test switches, communications, and integration with utility and applicable external metering systems.
Station AC and DC Auxiliary Systems
 – Design station service AC systems and DC control power systems, including station service transformers, transfer systems, panelboards, batteries, battery chargers, DC distribution panels, battery sizing calculations, and associated monitoring and alarms.
Grounding and Lightning Protection
 – Perform grounding system studies and design station grounding grids, equipment grounding, control building grounding, fence grounding, cable shielding and grounding, lightning shielding, surge protection, and related systems.
Electrical System Studies
 – Perform load flow, short circuit, voltage drop, equipment duty, insulation coordination, grounding, incident energy and arc flash, harmonic, and other electrical studies as required for the project.
Civil, Structural, and Geotechnical Engineering
 – Site grading, drainage, stormwater systems, access roads, oil containment, equipment foundations, control buildings, trenches, retaining structures, structural steel, equipment supports, fencing, seismic design, geotechnical coordination, and other civil/structural improvements required for receiving station and substation facilities.
Seismic Engineering
 – Evaluate and design station equipment, structures, anchorage, foundations, bus systems, and associated facilities for applicable seismic requirements, including IEEE 693 and applicable California Building Code requirements.
Cable and Conduit Systems
 – Design power, control, protection, instrumentation, and communications cable systems, including cable sizing, conduit sizing, conduit fill, pulling calculations, routing, cable schedules, trench systems, raceways, grounding, and separation requirements.
Outage and Construction Sequencing
 – Develop conceptual or detailed construction sequencing, temporary configurations, cutover plans, outage requirements, and energization sequences necessary to perform work at existing operating stations.
Equipment Specifications and Procurement Support
 – Prepare technical specifications and procurement documents for major station equipment; review vendor proposals, technical exceptions, shop drawings, calculations, test reports, and other vendor submittals; and provide technical assistance during equipment procurement.
Project Cost Estimating and Material Lists
 – Prepare planning level and detailed project cost estimates, bills of material, equipment lists, quantities, and other supporting documentation appropriate to the project phase.
Construction Documents and Specifications
 – Prepare complete engineering design packages including drawings, calculations, technical specifications, construction specifications, material requirements, equipment schedules, and other documents necessary for competitive bidding and construction.
Permitting and Agency Coordination
 – Provide engineering support for applicable permitting, utility coordination, environmental requirements, building permits, fire department requirements, and coordination with other governmental or regulatory agencies.
Construction Engineering Support
 – Respond to Requests for Information (RFIs), review contractor submittals and shop drawings, evaluate proposed substitutions, attend construction meetings, perform site visits, prepare design revisions, resolve field conditions, and provide other engineering support during construction.
Testing and Commissioning Support
 – Develop or review equipment testing, protection and control testing, functional testing, SCADA checkout, commissioning, energization, and acceptance requirements. Provide engineering support during station cutover, commissioning, and energization as required.
Record Drawings and Project Closeout
 – Review contractor redlines, prepare or review as-built drawings, incorporate field modifications into final engineering documents, and provide final calculations, settings, equipment documentation, and other project closeout records.
SCE Coordination
 – Coordinate the design of new or modified 230-kV facilities, if any, with Southern California Edison (SCE).
Coordination with Civil and Structural Engineering
 – For purposes of this Scope of Work, civil, structural, geotechnical, and seismic services generally address design integrated into a new or modified receiving station or substation design package. Civil and structural work issued as a standalone assignment, including vault inspection and evaluation, evaluation and retrofit of existing structures, and civil or structural design not part of a multidiscipline station design package, is included under Scope of Work 4, as determined by the City based on the requirements of the task order.

## Scope of Work 2: SCADA, Automation, Communications, and Control Design
Complete design of new and modified SCADA systems, substation automation systems, distribution automation systems, operational technology networks, communications systems, and associated control and monitoring facilities. Consultant shall have at least five (5) years of experience designing, integrating, configuring, testing, and commissioning electric utility SCADA, automation, communications, and control systems. Consultant shall have completed at least five (5) similar projects within the past five (5) years. Consultant staff shall include electrical, control systems, communications, networking, and cybersecurity engineering personnel, as applicable to the work being performed. Professional engineering services requiring registration shall be performed under the responsible charge of engineers registered in the State of California. Consultant shall have demonstrated experience integrating new systems into existing operating electric utility SCADA and operational technology environments. All work shall comply with PWP's applicable design criteria, standards, cybersecurity requirements, communications standards, and operating practices. SCADA, automation, communications, and control engineering services may include, but are not limited to:
SCADA Design
 – Design new or replacement SCADA systems, Remote Terminal Units (RTUs), concentrators, controllers, communications processors, input/output systems, protocol converters, and associated station SCADA equipment. Prepare system architecture diagrams, equipment layouts, wiring diagrams, I/O drawings, point lists, cable schedules, and equipment specifications.
Substation Automation
 – Design automation systems integrating protective relays, meters, intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), concentrators, controllers, and other station equipment. Develop automated control, monitoring, alarm, interlocking, sequence-of-events, and equipment-status functions.
Distribution Automation
 – Design and integrate automated distribution switches, reclosers, fault indicators, capacitor controls, voltage regulation equipment, and other field devices into PWP SCADA and communications systems. Provide associated control logic, communications, testing, and commissioning support.
SCADA Point Development and Database Engineering
 – Develop and verify SCADA point lists, analogs, status points, alarms, controls, quality flags, scaling, deadbands, engineering units, sequence-of-events requirements, and other database information required for integration with existing SCADA systems.
Communication Protocol Engineering
 – Design and configure communications using utility automation protocols including DNP3, IEC 61850, Modbus, IEC 60870, and other applicable protocols. Develop protocol mapping, data addressing, communications settings, report/control configuration, and protocol conversion requirements.
IEC 61850 and Digital Substation Systems
 – Develop IEC 61850 architectures and configurations, including station bus applications, GOOSE messaging, MMS communications, logical node mapping, datasets, reports, system configuration files, network architecture, and interoperability testing when required by the project.
Operational Technology Networking
 – Design utility operational technology Ethernet and IP networks, including switches, routers, firewalls, VLANs, network segmentation, redundancy, failover, addressing, routing, bandwidth requirements, quality of service, and network monitoring.
Fiber Optic Communications
 – Design fiber optic communications systems including fiber routes, cable selection, splice requirements, termination panels, patch panels, transceivers, optical budgets, communications equipment, and associated testing requirements.
Protective Relay Communications
 – Design communications interfaces supporting protective relaying applications, including line current differential, transfer trip, permissive tripping, blocking, relay-to-relay communications, synchrophasors, and other protection-related communication functions.
Time Synchronization
 – Design station time synchronization systems for protective relays, concentrators, controllers, meters, sequence-of-events recorders, and other intelligent devices using GPS-based or network-based time sources and applicable synchronization protocols.
SCADA Control and Interlocking Logic
 – Develop SCADA control permissives, interlocks, blocking logic, local/remote control logic, automatic transfer schemes, alarm logic, communications failure logic, and other programmable control functions necessary for safe and reliable system operation.
Programming and Configuration
 – Develop, modify, document, and test SCADA, concentrator, controller, communications processor, network equipment, and other programmable device configurations and logic.
Sequence-of-Events and Disturbance Data
 – Design systems for collection and transfer of sequence-of-events records, relay event reports, oscillography, fault records, and other operational data from intelligent electronic devices.
Operational Technology Cybersecurity
 – Incorporate cybersecurity requirements into SCADA and automation system designs, including network segmentation, firewalls, access control, secure remote access, user authentication, logging, device hardening, configuration management, and other cybersecurity measures applicable to the project.
Remote Engineering and Maintenance Access
 – Design secure methods for authorized engineering and field remote access to SCADA, relays, meters, concentrators, controllers, network equipment, and other station devices for engineering, maintenance, troubleshooting, and event retrieval.
System Architecture and Standardization
 – Develop or update standard SCADA, automation, networking, communications, concentrator, and controller architectures, typical drawings, device configurations, naming conventions, addressing standards, and engineering templates.
Existing System Evaluation and Modernization
 – Evaluate existing SCADA, concentrators, controllers, communications, networking, and automation equipment for obsolescence, reliability, capacity, cybersecurity, interoperability, and maintainability, and develop replacement or migration recommendations.
Equipment Specifications and Procurement Support
 – Prepare technical specifications for SCADA software, SCADA hardware, concentrators, controllers, network switches, routers, firewalls, communications processors, GPS clocks, radios, fiber optic equipment, servers, and other automation and communications equipment. Review vendor proposals, technical exceptions, drawings, and submittals.
Factory Acceptance Testing
 – Develop test procedures and provide engineering support for factory acceptance testing of SCADA, concentrators, controllers, automation, communications, networking, and integrated control systems.
System Integration Testing
 – Perform or support end-to-end testing between field devices, protective relays, concentrators, controllers, communications networks, SCADA nodes, operator interfaces, and other interconnected systems.
Site Acceptance Testing and Commissioning
 – Develop and execute testing procedures for installation verification, communications checkout, point-to-point testing, control testing, alarm verification, protocol testing, failover testing, and commissioning of SCADA and automation systems.
Cutover and Migration Planning
 – Develop detailed implementation, cutover, rollback, and migration plans for modifications to SCADA and communications systems to minimize interruption of system monitoring and control.
Troubleshooting and Technical Support
 – Provide engineering support for SCADA, communications, networking, automation, protocol, timing, concentrator, and controller problems, including troubleshooting intermittent or complex system performance issues.
Documentation and Record Drawings
 – Prepare and maintain system architecture drawings, network diagrams, IP address schedules, communications diagrams, equipment configuration records, logic diagrams, point lists, I/O databases, cable schedules, configuration backups, test records, and final as-built documentation.

## Scope of Work 3: System Planning
Complete system planning studies, technical analysis, and compliance support for the PWP electric system. Consultant shall have at least five (5) years of experience performing electric utility system planning studies and shall have completed at least five (5) similar projects within the past five (5) years. Consultant staff shall include electrical engineering personnel and, where NERC/WECC compliance or system operating work is performed, NERC-certified personnel, as applicable to the work being performed. Professional engineering services requiring registration shall be performed under the responsible charge of engineers registered in the State of California. All work shall comply with PWP's applicable design criteria, planning criteria, and operating practices. System planning services may include, but are not limited to:
Grid Modeling
 – Develop, update, and validate system models in PSLF to ensure compliance with NERC, WECC, CAISO, SCE, and other applicable requirements.
Compliance Program Support
 – Assist in drafting, auditing, and providing technical recommendations for utility programs and policy documentation, including:
Underfrequency load shedding programs
NERC CIP compliance
Physical security plans
Cybersecurity policies
Emergency response plans
Distribution and Subtransmission Engineering Studies
 – Conduct power flow analysis, short circuit duty analysis, reactive power analysis, N-1 studies, and contingency planning to identify system constraints and confirm that voltage, thermal, and operational criteria are met. Studies shall be performed in Milsoft WindMil for distribution studies and SKM PowerTools for substation and subtransmission studies.
Interconnection and System Impact Studies
 – Perform System Impact Studies and Facilities Studies for large loads, such as large commercial loads and data centers, and cluster or system-wide studies evaluating the combined impact of generation and battery energy storage interconnection requests. Identify grid capacity constraints, evaluate thermal, voltage, and operational impacts, and propose system mitigation measures for interconnection customers.
Distributed Energy Resource Integration and Hosting Capacity
 – Evaluate the ability of PWP's distribution and subtransmission systems to accommodate distributed generation, battery energy storage systems, electric vehicle loads, and other distributed energy resources (DERs). Perform hosting capacity, feeder capability, voltage, thermal loading, protection, reverse power flow, and other system-level analyses necessary to identify opportunities and constraints associated with increasing DER penetration. Develop planning recommendations for system upgrades, operational strategies, protection modifications, voltage regulation, and other measures necessary to support reliable DER integration. Support development of planning assumptions, scenarios, forecasts, and technical criteria for future deployment of solar generation, energy storage, and other DERs.
Load Forecasting and Master Planning
 – Develop system load forecasts and identify current and future system vulnerabilities, capacity deficits, operational constraints, and age-driven asset risks across distribution and subtransmission networks. Translate needs assessment findings into long-term capital improvement plans, resource adequacy analysis, and project prioritization. Recommend asset replacement schedules, risk-based prioritization, and phased execution timelines based on identified critical needs and resource limitations.
Reliability and Outage Root Cause Analysis
 – Perform root cause analysis on major system outages and equipment failures. Conduct overcurrent coordination studies, review trip settings, and recommend updates to enhance system reliability.
Grid Modernization
 – Provide technical recommendations and settings for distribution automation, fault location, isolation, and service restoration (FLISR), and other substation automation programs.
Technical Consulting and System Selection
 – Support the technical selection, scoping, and implementation of modern utility systems, such as:
Outage management system (OMS)
Distributed energy resource management system (DERMS)
Advanced engineering analysis software
Coordination with Renewable Energy and Energy Storage
 – For purposes of this Scope of Work, interconnection services generally address system planning and system-wide impacts. Project-specific interconnection feasibility studies, system impact studies, engineering, design, owner's engineering, implementation, and lifecycle support for an individual renewable generation, energy storage, or other inverter-based resource project are included under Scope of Work 6, as determined by the City based on the requirements of the task order.

## Scope of Work 4: Civil and Structural Engineering
Complete civil and structural design for utility infrastructure construction, improvements, modifications, and retrofits, including new facilities and modifications to existing facilities. Consultant shall have at least five (5) years of experience designing new, or modifying existing, civil and structural infrastructure and shall have completed at least five (5) similar projects within the past five (5) years. Consultant staff shall include civil, structural, and geotechnical engineering personnel, as applicable to the work being performed. Professional engineering services requiring registration shall be performed under the responsible charge of engineers registered in the State of California. All work shall comply with PWP's applicable design criteria and standards, PWP structural design criteria, applicable IEEE standards (including IEEE 693), ASCE 7, AISC, ACI, and California Building Code requirements. Civil and structural engineering services may include, but are not limited to:
Existing Conditions Assessment and Field Verification
 – Investigate, measure, and document existing structures and foundations where record drawings are missing, incomplete, or unverified. Develop existing-conditions drawings and models sufficient to support analysis and design of modifications and retrofits, and identify assumptions and residual risk where field verification cannot fully establish existing conditions.
Research
 – Collect and review record drawings, as-built information, geotechnical data, equipment weights, dimensions, seismic qualification and loading data, applicable codes and standards, PWP structural design criteria, and site-specific seismic and wind parameters.
Structural Modeling
 – Develop structural analysis models for open-air racks and bus structures, equipment support structures, foundations, and anchorage, including representation of equipment loads, seismic mass, short-circuit mechanical forces, and existing structural conditions.
Structural Analysis
 – Perform structural analysis for dead, live, wind, seismic (IEEE 693 and California Building Code), short-circuit mechanical, and equipment operating loads. Evaluate and load rate existing structures, including building rooftops, for added, modified, or reused loading, and check the adequacy of members, connections, anchorage, and foundations.
Structural Design
 – Design and detail new and modified structures, including substation open-air racks, steel equipment support structures, concrete pad and pier foundations, transformer and switchgear foundations and pads, seismic anchorage and restraint, retaining walls, screening walls, physical barriers, and associated connections. Prepare structural drawings, calculations, technical specifications, and material lists.
Site Grading, Drainage, and Stormwater Design
 – Design site grading, drainage, and stormwater systems.
Underground Civil Design
 – Design underground civil infrastructure, including vaults and duct systems.
Geotechnical Engineering
 – Provide geotechnical engineering and coordination.
Vault Inspection and Evaluation
 – Inspect and evaluate existing vaults for as-found condition and provide repair recommendations, technical specifications, and cost estimates. A construction or field contractor will perform physical repairs; Consultant provides inspection, evaluation, and recommendations only.
Coordination with Receiving Station and Substation Design
 – For purposes of this Scope of Work, services generally address civil and structural work issued as a standalone assignment, including evaluation, modification, and retrofit of existing structures, and civil and structural design not part of a multidiscipline station design package. Civil, structural, geotechnical, and seismic design integrated into a new or modified receiving station or substation design package is included under Scope of Work 1, as determined by the City based on the requirements of the task order.

(2) Violation; liability for unpaid wages; liquidated damages. In the event of any violation of the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section the contractor and any subcontractor responsible therefor shall be liable for the unpaid wages. In addition, such contractor and subcontractor shall be liable to the United States (in the case of work done under contract for the District of Columbia or a territory, to such District or to such territory), for liquidated damages. Such liquidated damages shall be computed with respect to each individual laborer or mechanic, including watchmen and guards, employed in violation of the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section, in the sum of $27 for each calendar day on which such individual was required or permitted to work in excess of the standard workweek of forty hours without payment of the overtime wages required by the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(1) of this section. (3) Withholding for unpaid wages and liquidated damages. The (write in the name of the Federal agency or the loan or grant recipient) shall upon its own action or upon written request of an authorized representative of the Department of Labor withhold or cause to be withheld, from any moneys payable on account of work performed by the contractor or subcontractor under any such contract or any other Federal contract with the same prime contractor, or any other federally-assisted contract subject to the Contract Work Hours and Safety Standards Act, which is held by the same prime contractor, such sums as may be determined to be necessary to satisfy any liabilities of such contractor or subcontractor for unpaid wages and liquidated damages as provided in the clause set forth in paragraph (b)(2) of this section. ## Scope of Work 6: Renewable Energy, Energy Storage, Interconnection, and Technical Advisory Services
Provide engineering design, technical studies, owner’s engineering, technical advisory, project development, procurement support, implementation support, commissioning, and lifecycle technical support for utility-scale and distributed renewable generation, battery energy storage systems (BESS), municipal solar and storage facilities, microgrids, resilience projects, and other inverter-based resources interconnected to PWP distribution, subtransmission, and receiving station facilities.
Consultant shall have at least five (5) years of relevant experience performing renewable generation, energy storage, interconnection engineering, or related technical advisory services and shall have completed at least five (5) similar projects within the past five (5) years. Consultant staff shall include electrical, civil, structural, and other engineering personnel, as applicable to the work being performed. Professional engineering services requiring registration shall be performed under the responsible charge of engineers registered in the State of California. Consultant shall demonstrate experience with renewable generation and energy storage projects and interconnections to operating electric utility systems, including municipal, distributed, and/or utility-scale resources, as applicable to the services being performed.
All work shall comply with PWP's applicable design criteria, interconnection requirements, protection and control standards, SCADA and communications standards, operating practices, and applicable IEEE, ANSI, NESC, NEC, California Building Code, California Fire Code, and other applicable industry standards.
Renewable energy, energy storage, interconnection, and technical advisory services may include, but are not limited to:
Feasibility, Site Assessment, and Project Development
 – Evaluate potential sites and existing facilities for renewable generation, BESS, microgrids, and related distributed energy resources. Services may include field investigations; evaluation of rooftop, ground-mount, parking canopy, parking structure, reservoir, and other installation opportunities; review of facility electrical infrastructure and load information; conceptual layouts; preliminary sizing; constructability assessments; identification of zoning, permitting, environmental, interconnection, building, electrical, and fire-code constraints; evaluation of applicable grants, incentives, and funding opportunities; planning-level cost estimates; and development of project implementation recommendations.
Owner’s Engineering and Technical Advisory Services
 – Provide independent technical advice and owner’s engineering services throughout planning, development, procurement, design, construction, commissioning, and operation of renewable generation and energy storage projects. Services may include technical due diligence, design criteria development, technical risk evaluation, project alternatives analysis, constructability review, value engineering, and review of technical assumptions and project performance requirements.
Utility-Scale and Distributed Solar Generation
 – Perform engineering associated with photovoltaic generation facilities, including electrical collection systems, inverters, DC and AC systems, medium-voltage systems, transformers, switchgear, protection, controls, grounding, metering, SCADA, communications, and utility interconnection facilities.
Battery Energy Storage Systems
 – Perform engineering associated with BESS facilities, including batteries, inverters, transformers, medium-voltage collection systems, switchgear, protection and control systems, grounding, auxiliary power systems, thermal management, fire protection, metering, SCADA, communications, and utility interconnection facilities.
Microgrids and Resilience Projects
 – Evaluate, plan, and design microgrid and resilience applications integrating generation, energy storage, facility loads, controls, communications, utility interfaces, and other distributed energy resources. Services may include operating-mode development, islanding strategies, load prioritization, black-start considerations, control philosophy, and resilience assessments.
Other Inverter-Based Resources
 – Evaluate and design interconnections for hybrid renewable and energy storage facilities and other existing or emerging inverter-based generation and energy technologies.
Energy and Facility Analysis
 – Review facility billing data, interval load data, existing service capacity, electrical distribution systems, panel capacities, transformer loading, and other available information necessary to evaluate project feasibility, system sizing, interconnection readiness, and potential facility upgrades.
Solar Resource and Performance Analysis
 – Perform solar resource assessment, shading analysis, energy production modeling, performance simulations, equipment comparisons, and other analysis necessary to evaluate photovoltaic system production and performance.
Photovoltaic Facility Design
 – Perform module selection, inverter sizing, string and combiner configuration, DC and AC electrical design, grounding, equipment layout, conductor sizing, voltage-drop calculations, and related photovoltaic engineering.
Structural Mounting Design 
– Perform structural evaluation and design for ground-mounted, rooftop, carport, parking-structure, reservoir, and other photovoltaic installations, including structural load evaluation of existing facilities and identification of required reinforcement or modifications.
Site Civil Design
 – Provide grading, drainage, access, paving, fencing, security, equipment pads, trenches, duct systems, stormwater, and other civil design associated with renewable generation and energy storage facilities.
Environmental and Permitting Support 
– Provide technical support for environmental review, permitting, zoning, building permits, fire department requirements, and coordination with applicable governmental or regulatory agencies.
Fire Access and Fire Code Compliance
 – Develop fire access, equipment spacing, emergency response, signage, hazard mitigation, and other design requirements associated with photovoltaic and battery energy storage installations.
Interconnection Standards Compliance 
– Perform interconnection design and technical studies in accordance with PWP requirements, IEEE 1547, and other applicable interconnection standards and requirements.
Project-Specific Interconnection Feasibility and System Impact Studies
 – Evaluate proposed generation and energy storage projects and their interconnections to determine impacts on the PWP electric system, including available system capacity, voltage performance, equipment loading, short-circuit duty, protection requirements, power quality, and required system upgrades.
Power System Studies
 – Perform load flow, short circuit, voltage regulation, protective device coordination, grounding, equipment duty, harmonic, power-quality, incident-energy, arc-flash, and other electrical studies necessary to evaluate and design renewable generation and energy storage facilities and their interconnections.
Inverter-Based Resource Studies 
– Evaluate inverter characteristics and operating modes, including fault-current contribution, reactive-power capability, voltage and frequency response, ride-through requirements, control interactions, harmonics, resonance, and other inverter-based resource performance.
Interconnection Point and Configuration Evaluation
 – Evaluate alternative points of interconnection, voltage levels, transformer configurations, switching arrangements, equipment ratings, conductor and cable requirements, and system modifications necessary to accommodate proposed projects.
Utility Interconnection Facilities
 – Design PWP utility interface facilities required to interconnect generation and energy storage projects, including circuit breakers, switchgear, transformers, disconnect switches, instrument transformers, surge arresters, bus systems, underground cable systems, overhead connections, and associated equipment.
Substation and Receiving Station Modifications
 – Develop modifications to existing substations and receiving stations necessary to accommodate renewable generation or energy storage projects, including expansion of buses, switchgear, protection and control systems, station auxiliary systems, metering, SCADA, communications, and other station facilities.
Protection and Control
 – Develop protective relaying and control requirements for generation and energy storage interconnections, including transformer, feeder, line, bus, breaker-failure, anti-islanding, abnormal-voltage, abnormal-frequency, synchronism, transfer-trip, and other protection functions, as applicable.
Protection Coordination and Relay Settings
 – Perform protection studies and develop or review relay settings required for reliable coordination between interconnected resources and the PWP electric system.
Grounding and Ground-Fault Protection
 – Evaluate system grounding configurations and develop grounding and ground-fault protection requirements for transformers, inverter systems, medium-voltage collector systems, switchgear, and utility interconnection facilities.
SCADA, Control, and Communications Integration
 – Develop requirements for monitoring and control of interconnected renewable generation and energy storage facilities, including remote status, alarms, analog values, controls, operating modes, communications interfaces, protocol requirements, and integration with existing PWP SCADA and operational technology systems.
Revenue and Operational Metering
 – Design and specify utility revenue, settlement, operational, and check-metering systems, including instrument transformers, meter panels, test switches, communications, and associated interfaces.
Telemetering and Operational Data
 – Develop requirements for real-time telemetry, equipment status, power flow, voltage, reactive power, state-of-charge, availability, alarms, and other operational information required by PWP or applicable balancing authority, transmission operator, or market entities.
Power Quality and Harmonic Evaluation
 – Evaluate harmonic distortion, flicker, voltage variation, inverter switching effects, resonance, and other power-quality impacts and recommend mitigation where required.
Equipment Ratings and Specifications
 – Develop or review technical requirements for photovoltaic modules, inverters, batteries, transformers, switchgear, circuit breakers, medium-voltage equipment, instrument transformers, grounding equipment, metering equipment, communications equipment, and other equipment associated with renewable generation, energy storage, and interconnection facilities.
Design Review of Developer or Contractor Facilities
 – Review drawings, calculations, studies, equipment specifications, protection schemes, controls, grounding, metering, SCADA, communications, and other technical documents prepared by developers, contractors, or their consultants for compliance with PWP requirements and applicable project criteria.
Interconnection Requirements and Technical Specifications
 – Develop project-specific interconnection requirements, technical specifications, design criteria, interface requirements, and utility standards for generation and energy storage facilities.
Utility System Upgrade Requirements 
– Identify and develop conceptual or detailed designs for PWP system upgrades necessary to support an interconnection, including substation, subtransmission, distribution, protection, communications, and control system improvements.
Construction Documents and Specifications
 – Prepare drawings, calculations, equipment specifications, construction specifications, material requirements, cost estimates, and other documents necessary for procurement, competitive bidding, and construction of renewable generation, energy storage, interconnection facilities, and associated system upgrades.
Construction and Outage Sequencing
 – Develop construction sequencing, temporary configurations, cutover plans, outage requirements, and energization sequences necessary to integrate new renewable generation and energy storage facilities.
Construction Engineering and Implementation Support
 – Respond to Requests for Information (RFIs), review contractor and developer submittals, plans, drawings, schedules, proposed substitutions, and change-related technical documentation; attend construction meetings; perform site observations; evaluate field conditions; and provide other engineering and owner’s support during construction.
Factory and Site Acceptance Testing 
– Develop or review testing requirements and procedures for major electrical equipment, protection and control systems, metering, SCADA, communications, inverters, BESS equipment, and other systems associated with the project or interconnection.
Commissioning and Energization 
– Develop or review commissioning, startup, acceptance, and energization plans and provide engineering support for point-to-point testing, relay testing, functional testing, inverter and battery testing, communications checkout, SCADA testing, meter verification, interconnection testing, and initial energization.
Operational Performance Verification
 – Support post-energization verification of renewable generation and energy storage performance, including energy production, active and reactive power response, voltage control, power-factor control, ramp rates, state-of-charge controls, alarms, communications, contractual performance requirements, and other operating requirements.
Operations, Performance, and Asset Management Support 
– Provide technical guidance regarding operation, maintenance, monitoring, and lifecycle management of renewable generation and energy storage facilities. Services may include review of monitoring data, production reports, maintenance records, service agreements, warranty claims, equipment condition, performance trends, preventive maintenance practices, equipment replacement strategies, and system optimization.
Technical Reporting and Stakeholder Support
 – Prepare technical memoranda, reports, presentations, project status information, and other technical materials and participate in meetings with City staff and other project stakeholders, as requested.
Coordination with System Planning
 – For purposes of this Scope of Work, interconnection studies generally address individual renewable generation, energy storage, or other inverter-based resource projects. Cluster and system-wide studies, large load interconnection studies, hosting capacity analysis, and long-term system planning are included under Scope of Work 3, as determined by the City based on the requirements of the task order.
Coordination with Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure
 – Provide technical coordination where renewable generation or energy storage projects interface with EV charging infrastructure or charging loads. Detailed EV charging infrastructure design is included under Scope of Work 5, as determined by the City based on the requirements of the task order.
Record Drawings and Project Closeout 
– Review contractor and developer redlines; prepare or review as-built drawings; incorporate field modifications; and provide final studies, relay settings, equipment documentation, test reports, commissioning documentation, O&M information, and other project closeout records.

SUMMARY: 
The Office of Management and Budget is revising the OMB Guidance for Grants and Agreements. The revisions are limited in scope to support implementation of the Build America, Buy America Act provisions of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and to clarify existing provisions related to domestic preferences. These revisions provide further guidance on implementing the statutory requirements and improve Federal financial assistance management and transparency. 
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 
Executive Summary 
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) is revising its guidance in title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations (2 CFR) to add a new part 184 and revise 2 CFR 200.322. The revisions implement the requirement for the Director of OMB to issue guidance to the head of each Federal agency to assist in the implementation of the requirements of the Build America, Buy America Act (BABA), Public Law 117-58, 135 Stat. 429, 70901-70927, Nov. 15, 2021. As required by BABA, the new part 184 of 2 CFR provides clear and consistent guidance to Federal agencies about how to apply the domestic content procurement preference (Buy This document is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on 08/23/2023 and available online at federalregister.gov/d/2023-17724, and on govinfo.gov America or BABA preference) as set forth in BABA to Federal awards for infrastructure projects. See BABA 70915. For example, the new part 184 includes definitions for key terms, including iron or steel products, manufactured products, construction materials, and materials identified in section 70917(c) (section 70917(c) materials) of BABA. These definitions provide a common system for Federal agencies to distinguish between the product categories established under the statutory text in BABA. The new part also offers standards that define “all manufacturing processes” in the case of construction materials. The new part 184 also includes guidance for determining the cost of components of manufactured products. The part 184 text uses a modified version of the “cost of components” test found in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) at 48 CFR 25.003, which is used for Federal procurement. Using this approach for determining the cost of components of manufactured products in the context of Federal financial assistance aims to provide a consistent approach for industry, with only minor modifications which are explained in this document. The new part 184 also includes guidance on proposing and issuing Buy America waivers. For example, based on the statutory text of BABA, it restates the circumstances under which a waiver may be justified. The new part also includes guidance on the type of process that a Federal agency should implement to allow recipients to request waivers, including the process a Federal agency should follow in issuing proposed and final waivers. The revised provision in 2 CFR part 200 specifies that Federal agencies providing Federal financial assistance for infrastructure projects must implement the Buy America preferences set forth in 2 CFR part 184, as required under section 70914(a) BABA, as of the effective date of the guidance, unless specified otherwise.

1.1     Request For Proposals
The Rose Bowl Operating Company (“RBOC”) is seeking to retain a qualified architectural firm to serve as its Venue Architect, a long-term design partner capable of providing site condition assessments, conceptual planning, pre-design and concept design, schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding, and construction administration, together with budget construction estimates throughout, for anticipated improvements, as well as providing presentation materials for visual and oral presentations to RBOC Board. RBOC’s current architectural services agreement expires December 31, 2026; this procurement will establish a successor agreement and position the organization to advance future capital improvements throughout the Rose Bowl campus. The selected firm will be considered to provide architectural services in connection with the various capital improvement projects that the RBOC may undertake, under multiple potential delivery methods, including Design-Bid-Build, Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR), and Design-Build. At this time the RBOC does not have identified funding for all such projects, but nonetheless must secure such services at this time so as to be able to move quickly when and if funding is secured. Any and all capital improvement projects are subject to the availability of funds and the approval of the RBOC.
RBOC anticipates issuing a written Notice to Proceed to the selected firm on or about January 4, 2027, authorizing the firm to begin performance of services while the definitive Services Contract is finalized; any services performed prior to full execution of the definitive Services Contract will be performed at the selected firm's own risk, subject to and governed by the terms of that contract upon execution.

1.2.1     Anticipated Capital Projects
As part of this procurement, RBOC will seek pricing and service approaches related to its anticipated capital improvement program. The Venue Architect is expected to serve as a long-term partner capable of supporting these and future projects across their full lifecycle. Anticipated projects include, but are not limited to:
1.2.1.1        East / West Seating Improvement Project. This project will replace the existing pink seating on both sides of the Bowl, West Section (Tunnels 1 through 8) and East Section (Tunnels 15 through 22). The project's principal driver is that the existing seats are not ADA compliant; the goal is larger, ADA-compliant seating, which will require the Architect to evaluate and design a reconfigured seating tier and tread, including elimination of the third row within each tier where necessary to accommodate the larger seats. The Architect shall also evaluate the potential addition of new center-line access aisles, stairs and handrails, within each seating section. Anticipated Design-Bid-Build or Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR) delivery, with the Design Team's efforts anticipated between January 2027 and December 2028, and a schedule targeting a January 2, 2029 construction start (subject to change) 
1.2.1.2        North Videoboard Expansion Project. This project will replace the existing videoboard configuration, consisting of one large center videoboard and two smaller flanking boards, with a single new videoboard. The Architect shall evaluate and recommend whether the new videoboard should be mounted consistent with the current configuration or integrated further into the stadium structure, and shall coordinate structural engineering as part of the design. The overall height of the videoboard structure is to remain consistent with the existing installation, in order to preserve sightlines to the surrounding mountains and minimize impacts to neighboring properties. Design efforts for this project may potentially commence in January 2027, concurrent with the East / West Seating Improvement Project, though the design start date remains to be determined. Anticipated CMAR or Design-Build delivery, with a schedule targeting a January 2, 2029 construction start (subject to change), consistent with the East / West Seating Improvement Project.
1.2.1.3        Other Projects. Additional capital improvement projects to be determined as RBOC’s capital plan advances.
